biography.name: Elena Duarte

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger brother; an aunt nearby is a dental assistant. Family relationships are affectionate and occasionally noisy.
background.finances: Stable household income; extracurricular fees require choosing one paid activity at a time.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas; cousins live across the border and visit when arrangements permit.
background.cultureLanguages: Uses Spanish and English at home; reads recreationally mostly in English.
background.school: Large public high school; steady grades with particular patience for practical assignments.
background.accessOpportunities: Has library access, a shared home laptop, inexpensive craft supplies, and occasional public clinic education events through her aunt.

timeline.story: At four Elena spent long afternoons making tiny beds for plastic animals while her brother knocked them over. She liked the folding and taping more than the pretend conversations. Her father let her sort washers in the garage, although he stopped her taking the smallest ones into the yard.

In first grade she enjoyed reading aloud when she had rehearsed the page. Unplanned speaking made her cheeks hot. She and a cousin traded elaborate paper bracelets and argued about whose knots held. At home, brushing teeth was mainly a chore she tried to shorten before cartoons.

At eight she needed several fillings. The unfamiliar sounds frightened her, but she watched a staff member assemble a demonstration tray afterward. Her aunt showed her a large teaching model, never real patient materials. Elena wanted to know why a hard tooth could have a soft inside.

Between ten and eleven she remade a broken doll hinge using thread, wire, and repeated attempts. Her teacher praised the repair; Elena was more pleased that it moved evenly. She also followed videos about teeth and digestion, skipping the presenters who turned every explanation into a loud joke.

Braces brought soreness, complaints, and a new habit of studying her mouth in a small mirror. She became good at cleaning around awkward spaces but often postponed starting. A close friend sent dramatic treatment clips; Elena asked her to stop because she disliked the fear-based commentary and surprise blood.

At fourteen she helped prepare paper packets for a public oral-health event and practiced using oversized floss on a plastic model. She liked explaining one concrete step. When a small child cried, she froze and fetched her aunt. She still enjoyed the afternoon and did not want to pretend otherwise.

Now sixteen, she repairs costume jewelry for two friends and can keep her hands steady through slow, fiddly work. Her aunt says she should consider following her example. Elena likes the objects and explanations but does not know whether she would enjoy strangers being uncomfortable all day. She also wants weekends for volleyball.

avoids: Being expected to calm every upset child
activities: Helps her brother organize school supplies
demonstratedSkills: Makes secure small joins after practice
motivations: Understanding what is happening inside a body
ambitions: Wants to buy her own reliable laptop
Considering an advanced biology class
practicalConstraints: One paid activity at a time

biography.selfDescription: I like little things being right. That sounds fussy. I can leave my laundry everywhere, so apparently it only counts for some things. People say I am gentle because I am quiet, but being quiet does not mean I know what to say. I want to keep learning the tooth stuff. I do not want every adult conversation to end with a decision about my whole life.
openQuestions: Would repeated contact with upset people become easier or remain draining?
Does she enjoy biological explanations beyond familiar mouth-related examples?

biography.name: Jamal Whitaker

background.family: Lives with his mother, grandfather, and older sister; father lives in another Texas city and calls regularly.
background.finances: Rent and basics are usually covered; extra work hours sometimes disrupt family plans.
background.geography: San Antonio, Texas; previously lived in Waco.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family with church connections; Jamal attends for relatives and music more than certainty about belief.
background.school: Public high school; plays trombone and receives ordinary classroom support for organization.
background.accessOpportunities: Library internet, school music lending program, family health appointments, and limited transport after school.

timeline.story: Jamal remembers building couch forts with his sister and asking his grandfather to be the monster. His grandfather usually fell asleep halfway through. Jamal liked replaying the same chase with a different ending, and he was furious when adults suggested that he was getting too big for the game.

At six he learned to make toast and carry a cup without spilling. His mother praised his careful walking, but school worksheets vanished in his backpack. He wanted to sit beside older cousins at family gatherings, listening to stories even when he did not understand why everyone laughed.

His grandfather developed a recurring leg wound when Jamal was eight. Adults handled treatment. Jamal asked why skin sometimes closed and sometimes did not, then forgot the question when a neighbor brought a scooter. Later he drew a lopsided diagram after finding a library book about circulation.

At ten he started trombone because the school could lend one. He disliked the first months of cracked notes but loved being inside a loud group. During his grandfather’s appointments he kept him company and wrote down questions the adults wanted to remember, without deciding which treatment was appropriate.

A move to San Antonio at twelve separated him from his closest friend. They played online most evenings until their schedules drifted. He became more interested in how infection spreads after a classroom experiment, but his lab reports were incomplete because he enjoyed discussion and neglected the written conclusion.

At fourteen he regularly prepared his grandfather’s lunch and checked whether a requested item was within reach. He resented missing band socials, then felt guilty about resenting it. His sister arranged a schedule so he was not the automatic helper. That made him more willing to sit and talk afterward.

At sixteen he can explain basic circulation from school and notices when his grandfather seems unusually tired, which he reports to an adult. He enjoys conversation with older people but finds repeated instructions irritating. He plans to finish high school with band and hopes to stay within visiting distance of family afterward.

avoids: Writing up work after the exciting part
demonstratedSkills: Keeps a practiced music part in time
motivations: Being useful without being taken for granted
ambitions: Finish high school with band
Live near relatives as a young adult
practicalConstraints: Household schedules depend on work shifts
Care tasks sometimes compete with practice

biography.selfDescription: I am good with my granddad because I know him. I do not know if that means I am good with old people generally. Biology makes sense when somebody draws it, and then I can say it back. A blank report page is different. Mostly I want a normal week where we know who is doing what and I get to play music without checking my phone every ten minutes.
openQuestions: How much of his enjoyment of care comes from this particular relationship?
Would structured writing support change his experience of science classes?

biography.name: Sofía Villarreal

background.family: Lives with her parents, grandmother, and two cousins during the school week; relatives share tasks on a small leased growing plot.
background.finances: Income varies by season and parents’ paid work; the family tracks supplies closely.
background.geography: Near Weslaco in the Rio Grande Valley, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English across home and school; grandmother prefers Spanish.
background.school: Public high school with an agricultural elective; math performance is steady while long reading assignments take more effort.
background.accessOpportunities: Direct experience with vegetables and chickens, borrowed tools, school internet, and limited access to paid camps.

timeline.story: At four Sofía helped her grandmother wash plastic buckets and made mud soup with a cousin. She loved the chickens until one chased her across the yard. For months she insisted on being carried past their pen, while still demanding to collect the warm eggs after an adult went in.

At six she kept a row of bean plants in reused cups. Some died because she watered all of them every time she remembered. Her grandmother explained the wet soil, but Sofía mainly wanted a replacement seed. She also liked racing bicycles on the short lane beside the house.

Between eight and nine she began comparing which plants wilted first. She could recognize several common weeds by sight but mixed up their names at school. At a roadside produce table she liked stacking colors and watching customers choose, although she hid behind her father when asked to make change.

At ten her father let her enter seed and feed purchases in a ruled notebook. She copied figures accurately when the receipts were legible and sometimes switched columns. Counting the remaining sacks helped her understand the mistake. She enjoyed that there was a physical thing to check against the number.

At twelve a sick chicken needed to be separated. Sofía helped prepare water and bedding but would not watch an adult examine its injury. She remained interested in eating, growth, and disease prevention without enjoying every part of animal care. Her cousin teased her, which made her refuse to discuss it.

At fourteen she took an agricultural elective and learned that classmates with similar family experience had very different equipment and free time. A friend posted polished growing videos; Sofía copied a labeling idea but abandoned filming because everyone at home interrupted. Her favorite success was reducing repeated trips for forgotten supplies.

Now sixteen she checks a weekly supplies list and can spot when an order exceeds available storage. She enjoys selling produce alongside her father but dislikes bargaining with people who treat her as a child. Her parents hope for a four-year college; she wants more training but has not agreed about distance or cost.

demonstratedSkills: Plans a workable sequence of errands
ambitions: Continue learning after high school
Help replace an unreliable irrigation timer
supports: Parents who include her in decisions

biography.selfDescription: I like growing things, except the phrase sounds cute and most of it is checking the same stuff again. I like that part too, sometimes. I am not brave about hurt animals. People act like that cancels knowing anything else. I might leave here for school. I might want to come back. I want enough information that it is an actual choice and not everybody arguing about a picture in their head.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy larger systems with less direct contact with plants?
What distance and training arrangements would feel workable to her?

biography.name: Noah Feld

background.family: Lives with two mothers and a younger sister; one mother works in a hospital administration role and the other runs a small home bakery.
background.finances: Comfortable and predictable income; family can fund several enrichment experiences.
background.geography: Austin, Texas, with grandparents in Houston.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; celebrates Jewish family holidays and participates irregularly in congregation activities.
background.school: Public high school; enjoys business math and dislikes open-ended group projects.
background.accessOpportunities: Home computer, dependable transport, bakery records, public hospital learning events, and summer enrichment choices.

timeline.story: Noah spent preschool arranging toy groceries and making his mothers stand in line. He changed the prices whenever his sister grabbed something. Outside, he loved the splash pad and disliked sand in his shoes. Adults remembered his pretend shop more clearly than he did; he remembered being allowed to ring the bell.

At six he helped put stickers on cookie boxes, becoming annoyed when labels were crooked. He could not yet read every flavor name, so he matched pictures. His mother let him stop when he was bored. He also collected joke books and regularly ruined the punchlines by laughing too early.

At eight he began counting returned baking trays and keeping tally marks on scrap paper. He liked a finished count more than decorating cakes. A friend suggested selling their old toys, and Noah enjoyed setting out a table until a neighbor asked for a discount and he took it personally.

At ten he attended a public hospital family event because his mother worked nearby. He listened carefully to a handwashing demonstration and asked how equipment gets ordered. A caregiving role-play made him uncomfortable; he did not enjoy pretending to reassure somebody or discussing personal symptoms with an unfamiliar adult.

At twelve he entered bakery expenses into a practice spreadsheet with his mother checking every line. He liked finding duplicate entries and confidently announced a profit before remembering several missing costs. Being corrected embarrassed him. For a while he avoided the file, although he kept suggesting ways to organize orders.

At fourteen he helped at a community bake sale and discovered that he enjoyed short customer conversations with a clear purpose. A friend whose family faced illness talked about helping patients. Noah listened but did not share the attraction. He was relieved when the friend accepted that he could care about her without liking care work.

At sixteen he manages a mock inventory for a school club fundraiser and checks the actual boxes with another student. He enjoys choosing stock amounts and hates chasing late payments. His settled wish is to study subjects involving trade and records after school; the exact setting remains vague, and his confidence sometimes outruns his arithmetic.

demonstratedSkills: Builds a basic spreadsheet with checking
motivations: Visible evidence that a task is finished
ambitions: Study trade and financial records after high school
Save for a long cycling trip
practicalConstraints: Family requires adult review of real business figures

biography.selfDescription: I do like people, just in amounts with an ending. That sounds bad. I mean I like helping someone pick the right box and then we both know it is done. My mom says that is a real kind of helping. I do not want to talk about bodies all day. I want to learn enough about money that I stop making big announcements before counting everything.
openQuestions: How will he respond to financial work with fewer immediate answers?
Can he share responsibility without checking everyone’s work twice?

biography.name: Priya Menon

background.family: Lives with her father, stepmother, and an older stepbrother; sees her mother on agreed weekends.
background.finances: Stable finances; two households can both support activities but coordination takes effort.
background.geography: Plano, Texas; earlier childhood in Irving.
background.cultureLanguages: English is dominant; understands some Malayalam and uses a few familiar expressions with grandparents.
background.school: Public high school; swim team participant with uneven enthusiasm for academic competition.
background.accessOpportunities: Pool access, supervised safety courses, school resources, and reliable transport when schedules are coordinated.

timeline.story: Priya liked the apartment pool at four but refused to put her face in the water. Her father invented games with floating cups, and she gradually stopped needing him beside every step. At home she replayed animated films and assigned her stuffed animals parts, getting angry when adults changed their voices.

At six she joined lessons with a friend and discovered that she liked repetitive swimming better than the noisy games afterward. She was not the fastest child. Her instructor praised her willingness to try again, but Priya mostly remembers earning a snack and showing her mother the damp paper certificate.

At eight her parents separated. Switching bags between homes became a larger problem than either adult expected, especially when goggles were missing. Swimming remained enjoyable because the pool looked the same every week. She also spent cheerful weekends with cousins, whose elaborate outdoor games rarely involved any organized sport.

At ten she watched a lifeguard manage a minor poolside accident while another adult cleared space. The quiet directions interested her more than the injury. At a later supervised lesson she learned why people should call for trained help and avoid putting themselves in danger. She liked having an ordered first step.

At twelve she completed an introductory safety class using practice equipment and adult instruction. She remembered the sequence on a mannequin but spoke too softly in a paired drill. Her friend was louder and less accurate. Comparing them helped her notice that knowing steps and making yourself heard were separate problems.

At fourteen she swam on a school team and often timed practice laps for teammates. An online swimming group made every small setback sound disastrous, so she muted it during exams. When a teammate became dizzy, she summoned the coach and stayed nearby. The coach handled the situation; Priya felt shaky afterward.

Now sixteen she wants to complete the required training for a supervised pool job next summer if she meets the prerequisites. She likes swimming and concrete safety routines but does not enjoy being treated as the person who must always stay calm. She is practicing a firm speaking voice and still hates shouting across a room.

motivations: Knowing what first step is appropriate
ambitions: Complete eligible pool-job training next summer
Keep swimming after high school
supports: Friend who practices speaking with her

biography.selfDescription: I am calm-looking. Inside can be completely different. I like being told exactly what the practice situation is, but real life does not come with that part. I still want the training. Maybe I just want to be at the pool and get paid, which is also true. I do not have a big explanation for why swimming has stayed mine when I dropped so many other activities.
openQuestions: How will she experience responsibility during ordinary paid shifts?
Does practiced communication carry into unfamiliar situations?

biography.name: Mateo Ruiz

background.family: Lives with his mother, younger brother, and mother’s partner; an older cousin is a frequent visitor.
background.finances: Household is financially tight following reduced work hours; basics are met with little spare cash.
background.geography: Laredo, Texas; relatives in Corpus Christi and Nuevo Laredo.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish and English at home; comfortable switching in ordinary conversation, less confident with formal writing in either language.
background.school: Public high school; has made up missing work after a difficult transition to high school.
background.accessOpportunities: School Chromebook, public library, family receipt sorting, and a small neighborhood shop where he helps a known adult occasionally.

timeline.story: Mateo liked lining up toy buses and then making them crash into a pillow. His mother remembers the careful lines; he remembers the crashes. He spent evenings with cousins in the courtyard, inventing rules that changed when someone started losing. He liked being included and was rarely the one deciding the game.

At six he learned the walking route to a nearby shop beside his mother and memorized which houses had dogs. He liked carrying one small purchase home. School praise came mainly for finishing quietly, although he often copied the first instruction and missed the second when classmates were talking.

At eight he helped his mother put household receipts into envelopes. She checked all calculations. Mateo liked crossing a finished item off the list and once taped an empty envelope shut because it looked incomplete. An adult explained why looking tidy did not necessarily make a record accurate.

At ten he spent summer mornings with a shopkeeper his family knew. He arranged empty cartons and copied shelf labels, stopping when customers needed the aisle. He enjoyed the predictable opening routine. He disliked the afternoon crowd and preferred to go home for games with his brother once the shop became noisy.

At twelve a cousin showed him a budgeting app. Mateo entered fictional purchases for fun but lost interest when it required linking accounts, which he did not do. His school friend liked debating investing videos; Mateo was more interested in whether a price included delivery than in promises of quick gains.

At fourteen he missed assignments while trying to watch his brother and help with changing household schedules. He said school was pointless, although he was upset by failing marks. A teacher helped him build a short daily checklist. He improved through routine and reminders, without suddenly finding every subject interesting.

At sixteen he can reconcile a small list of purchases with receipts and flag missing entries for an adult. He enjoys setting up repeated work more than choosing new projects. Family members call him dependable, but he sometimes ignores messages when overwhelmed. He wants a steady adult life and cannot yet describe its contents.

activities: Checks household receipts with his mother
demonstratedSkills: Sets out materials in a familiar order
motivations: Having his own money without constant uncertainty
ambitions: Finish school on time
Have a steady adult routine; details unclear

biography.selfDescription: People say I am organized. My bag is not organized. I can organize a job if I know what the job is. Starting from nothing is harder. I do not have an inspiring answer about the future. A place to live, money for food, time to see people. I know that is not a whole plan. I wish people would let it be a beginning without laughing.
openQuestions: Would he enjoy record work when the procedures become more complex?
Which responsibilities are chosen and which reflect household need?

biography.name: Avery Coleman

background.family: Lives with their parents and older brother; grandparents nearby host frequent Sunday lunches.
background.finances: Comfortable finances and stable housing; family can usually afford chosen supplies.
background.geography: Denton, Texas; spends several weeks each summer with relatives near Tyler.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household; family accepts their pronouns, while a few distant relatives remain inconsistent.
background.school: Public high school; uses hearing aids and has agreed classroom accommodations.
background.accessOpportunities: Home internet, a small yard, public nature programs, library materials, and accessible seating arranged through school.

timeline.story: At four Avery loved watering the patch of dirt beneath a tree and searching for moving things afterward. They did not distinguish worms from roots at first. Their brother supplied dramatic names for every discovery. Avery also enjoyed indoor blanket forts, especially when rain made the backyard games impossible.

At six they received hearing aids and complained more about itchy ears than about the classroom changes adults discussed. A teacher offered a better seat and checked instructions privately. Avery kept bringing home leaves and once cried when a carefully saved caterpillar disappeared from an uncovered shoebox overnight.

At eight they borrowed an insect guide but mostly used the pictures. Their grandfather helped make a ventilated observation container and return small animals outdoors. Avery liked repeated observation and disliked being told to touch everything. They were happy to watch a spider from a distance without proving bravery.

At ten they kept a notebook of pill bugs found beneath the same stones. The drawings were rough and the dates fairly consistent. A cousin called the hobby boring; Avery agreed it probably looked boring and continued. They also spent hours playing cooperative building games with two friends from school.

At twelve a nature-program leader helped them compare observations without claiming that every difference meant a discovery. Avery had been excited about a pattern that disappeared when they checked again. They felt foolish for a week. The next summer they started another notebook, with fewer dramatic titles on the pages.

At fourteen they took biology and enjoyed learning how small organisms survive in changing conditions. Group discussions could be tiring when everyone spoke at once; this did not predict which activities they liked. They loved noisy family games when they could follow turns. They disliked babysitting, including the constant need to interpret someone else’s crying.

Now sixteen Avery checks a shaded yard corner after rain and joins nature walks when transport works. They can describe familiar organisms carefully but are unsure about identification beyond their guide. Friends encourage them to post videos; they prefer keeping notes private. Their current ambition is to take a more demanding biology class without dropping their game nights.

unfamiliarActivities: Extended field trips away from family
motivations: Having a private interest that is still taken seriously
ambitions: Take a more demanding biology class
Keep enough free time for friends
struggles: Pressure to turn hobbies into content
practicalConstraints: Listening fatigue can limit long group sessions
Most advanced equipment only available at school

biography.selfDescription: I like noticing things. I do not always know what they mean. People sometimes hear one fact and act like I am the bug expert, which is uncomfortable when I cannot identify the very bug they found. I also do normal boring phone stuff. I do not spend every evening in the dirt. I think I want more biology, but I want to find out what the harder class actually feels like.
openQuestions: Does curiosity persist through more formal laboratory reporting?
What mix of solitary observation and collaborative work suits them?

biography.name: Tessa Moreno

background.family: Lives with her father, grandmother, and three-year-old half-brother; stepmother works alternating out-of-town weeks.
background.finances: Household expenses are covered, but reliable paid childcare is difficult to arrange locally.
background.geography: Outside Abilene, Texas; long bus ride to school.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking home; family traditions center on extended-family meals and local events.
background.school: Small public high school; likes literature discussions and participates inconsistently in clubs.
background.accessOpportunities: Library books, school activities requiring advance transport plans, and substantial everyday contact with a toddler and older adult.

timeline.story: Tessa liked dancing in the kitchen while her grandmother cooked and collecting tiny shampoo bottles from family trips. Adults sometimes called her a little helper because she handed over spoons. She also threw spectacular tantrums when tired. Family videos remind her that being helpful was only one part of her childhood.

At six she liked reading the same picture book to younger cousins and making funny voices. She became cross when they skipped pages. Her father taught her to ride a bicycle in a parking lot, and she spent an entire summer trying to beat her own circuit time rather than racing anyone else.

At eight her grandmother had knee surgery. Tessa brought books and cups of water when asked, while adults handled treatment and mobility advice. She liked the long conversations during recovery. She also avoided the room some afternoons because the television was always on and she wanted the adults to watch her new tricks.

At ten she joined a library reading activity and discovered that some younger children wanted to talk instead of listen. She enjoyed inventing questions more than enforcing quiet. A librarian helped her end sessions at the scheduled time. Otherwise she kept staying because she worried leaving would look unfriendly.

At twelve her half-brother was born and she loved making him laugh. As he grew, short visits became regular responsibilities during changing work arrangements. Tessa could settle him with familiar songs, but she was not always glad to be available. A friend complained that every invitation required a family discussion.

At fourteen she helped run a supervised story hour and enjoyed it more than unplanned childcare at home. The clear start, finish, and available adults mattered. Online friends praised her for being mature, which felt good until she noticed she was hiding ordinary anger to keep that description. She stopped posting family updates so often.

At sixteen she still enjoys reading to children and talking with her grandmother. She has negotiated one protected afternoon each week, though emergencies sometimes swallow it. She wants to attend a residential program after high school and feels disloyal saying so. She is good at familiar care routines and unsure whether she wants more of them.

avoids: Being called mature as a reason to give her more work
activities: Literature discussion group when transport works
demonstratedSkills: Adapts familiar stories for younger listeners
Maintains patient conversation with her grandmother
ambitions: Attend a residential learning program after high school
Protect a weekly afternoon for friends
struggles: Anger she finds hard to admit
supports: Father increasingly willing to plan care

biography.selfDescription: I do love him. I hate starting with that every time I say I want to go somewhere. Reading with kids is fun when it is something I picked. At home sometimes it is fun too, and sometimes I count the minutes. I do not know what that says about me. I want to leave for a while and still be somebody my family can call, just maybe not for every little thing.
openQuestions: How would chosen, bounded care feel compared with family obligation?
Can her plan to study away become practically possible?

biography.name: Darius Bell

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; aunt and uncle nearby are involved in everyday life.
background.finances: Stable middle-income household; parents plan purchases carefully and support one travel sport.
background.geography: Fort Worth, Texas; family visits relatives in east Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family; basketball, cookouts, and church gatherings connect several generations.
background.school: Public high school; school basketball player with solid practical math performance.
background.accessOpportunities: Coaches, supervised injury rehabilitation, a recreation center, home internet, and occasional access to an uncle’s delivery-route planning.

timeline.story: Darius loved chasing bubbles and repeatedly climbing the same playground ladder. His sister was too small to join, so he assigned her the job of cheering from a blanket. His parents remember an energetic child, but he also spent long rainy mornings sorting sports cards with his uncle and arguing about made-up teams.

At six he joined a recreation basketball group because his best friend was there. He liked passing drills and hated waiting for games to begin. Losing could ruin the ride home. His mother eventually stopped analyzing each game with him, and their trips became easier when they talked about dinner instead.

At eight he began asking why muscles felt sore after running. A children’s body book supplied explanations he partly understood and repeated too confidently. He liked testing how far he could jump, then forgot to record most measurements. His interest was in moving and comparing, not in keeping a careful research notebook.

At ten he rode with his uncle during an approved daytime delivery outing. He enjoyed checking stop order and matching parcels to a printed list. The route changed after a closure, which seemed like a puzzle. He was less interested in the customer conversations and mostly wanted to see whether they could recover the lost time.

At twelve basketball became more serious. Video clips made him compare his body with older players, and he started taking criticism personally. A coach helped him focus on one controllable part of practice. He improved his foot placement through repetition, although he still disliked being corrected in front of teammates.

At fourteen a sprained ankle interrupted his season. Qualified adults directed treatment and rehabilitation; Darius tracked the assigned exercises and asked why particular movements were limited. He liked understanding recovery but hated the slow pace. He sometimes skipped the last set, then admitted this when asked instead of pretending the plan had failed.

At sixteen he is playing again and wants to finish a full healthy season while keeping his grades steady. He enjoys explaining a familiar warm-up to younger players with a coach present. He also helps plan family errands efficiently. He is curious about bodies and transport systems without assuming those interests belong together.

avoids: Slow repetitive recovery work when impatient
ambitions: Complete a healthy school season
Maintain grades while playing
practicalConstraints: Access to specialized body knowledge mostly through school or treatment

biography.selfDescription: I like knowing why an exercise is there. I do not always like doing it after I know why. Apparently those are separate things. I am not making a plan to play forever. Right now I want a season where I get to be on the court. People ask what else I am about and I feel like I have to invent something bigger than the stuff I already do.
openQuestions: Would interest in body mechanics continue outside sport and personal recovery?
Does route planning stay enjoyable when customer demands enter the problem?

biography.name: Linh Tran

background.family: Lives with her mother and maternal grandparents; father is involved from a nearby apartment.
background.finances: Modest, fairly steady income; larger purchases take saving and discussion.
background.geography: Garland, Texas; born in Texas and visits relatives in California occasionally.
background.cultureLanguages: English and conversational Vietnamese; grandparents sometimes help with vocabulary she does not know.
background.school: Public high school; receives reading accommodations for dyslexia and completes demanding practical work patiently.
background.accessOpportunities: School library audiobooks, inexpensive model kits, orthodontic appointments, and a community center handwork group.

timeline.story: At four Linh liked peeling stickers off sheets and placing them along the edges of cardboard boxes. Her grandfather showed her how to fold paper bags. She enjoyed walks to a small park and insisted on a particular swing. She was cheerful with familiar adults but would not perform songs for visitors.

At six reading lessons became frustrating while her hands seemed to learn folding patterns quickly. Adults sometimes praised the folding immediately after discussing school difficulties, which made it feel like consolation. She still liked the activity. Her father brought wordless puzzle books so they could share something without correcting her pronunciation.

At eight she received reading support and began enjoying stories through audio. At the community center she learned simple stitching, unpicked uneven rows, and sometimes abandoned pieces halfway through. A friend made faster, messier work and called hers overcareful. Linh secretly liked some of the friend’s loose, funny designs better.

At ten she had a loose tooth that refused to fall out and became fascinated by the permanent tooth appearing behind it. A dental visit answered some questions. She started noticing bite shapes in animal photographs but did not research systematically. Most evenings she preferred a comedy series with her grandmother.

At twelve orthodontic visits gave her another reason to ask about tooth movement and small adjustments. She liked a staff member explaining models without rushing. She practiced threading cord through tiny beads at home, a separate hobby that adults began connecting to her questions. Linh was unsure whether she agreed with their connection.

At fourteen she helped a supervised public oral-health table by assembling sealed take-home packets and demonstrating brushing on a large model after rehearsal. Reading the information aloud was tiring; pointing and answering familiar questions felt easier. She liked the precise demonstration but not the crowd, and she left earlier than she had expected.

At sixteen she can mend small tears neatly and assemble a model from illustrated directions. She asks good follow-up questions in appointments but has no experience with treatment tools. She wants to complete a complicated model ship and choose next year’s classes herself. Adults’ certainty about what her hands mean still irritates her.

avoids: Adults assigning meaning to every hobby
motivations: Completing something difficult at her own pace
ambitions: Finish a complicated model ship
Choose next year’s classes herself
supports: Father who shares puzzles without pressure
practicalConstraints: Needs accessible formats for long texts

biography.selfDescription: My hands are not a secret message about what I am supposed to become. I do like tiny work. I can also get sick of tiny work and shove it in a drawer for months. The mouth questions are interesting because the changes happen slowly and then you notice them. I wish I could say something is interesting without somebody immediately making a future out of it.
openQuestions: Does she want deeper biological study or mainly explanations of familiar experiences?
Which projects sustain her attention after novelty fades?

biography.name: Gabriel Okafor

background.family: Lives with both parents and two younger sisters; an uncle operates a small hardware store nearby.
background.finances: Secure household finances; parents fund school activities and occasional family travel.
background.geography: Katy, Texas; spent two early-childhood years in Lagos before returning to Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home with some Igbo phrases; extended-family calls connect relatives across several places.
background.school: Public high school; likes practical algebra and prefers defined group responsibilities.
background.accessOpportunities: Home computer, dependable transport, store stock exposure, school clubs, and parents willing to support different educational routes.

timeline.story: At four Gabriel liked toy trains, especially carrying blocks from one room to another in their wagons. His sisters were not yet old enough to join. At family gatherings he followed older cousins until they told him to leave. He remembers happy beach outings more clearly than the international move adults consider so significant.

At six he enjoyed classroom jobs such as putting away pencils, but only if everyone followed the same rule. He once made a classmate cry by confiscating an unsorted box. His teacher helped him return it and ask for cooperation. At home he was far less strict about his own scattered toys.

At eight his uncle let him place familiar hardware packages on low shelves during quiet hours. He liked matching labels and disliked the dusty floor. He also played soccer casually and was satisfied being an ordinary player. Winning did not interest him enough to practice alone after his friends went home.

At ten he watched his uncle count stock before ordering. Gabriel guessed that everything should be bought in equal numbers, then learned that shelves emptied at different rates. He began checking actual counts before making suggestions. He enjoyed the practical consequence of an answer more than simply getting a school calculation right.

At twelve he played a logistics game with online friends and became absorbed in avoiding bottlenecks. He also learned that keeping a game running efficiently could make his friends bored if he issued constant instructions. They set aside some evenings for unplanned play. Gabriel grumbled and eventually found those evenings fun too.

At fourteen he helped the school club organize event materials. His first inventory was too detailed for anyone else to maintain, so missing updates made it useless. Another student proposed a shorter sheet. Accepting the simpler version was difficult, but it improved the next event. They remained friends after arguing about it.

At sixteen he checks selected store stock alongside his uncle and understands when to flag an uncertain count. He likes the movement of goods and the arithmetic of orders. His parents expect further education but do not insist on a particular subject. Gabriel wants substantial practical study and is comparing programs without a settled destination.

avoids: Maintaining excessive detail after it stops helping
motivations: Useful systems others will actually use
Independence while retaining close family ties
ambitions: Continue practical study after high school
Learn to manage a larger real project
practicalConstraints: Store tasks limited to approved hours and safe areas

biography.selfDescription: I like a system when it works for the actual people. I did not always remember the people part. Sometimes I still want to explain why my sheet was technically better, even when nobody used it. I am pretty sure I want more study after school. I am less sure which kind. My family asks about that a lot, but they also let me take my time answering.
openQuestions: How does he handle routine work that includes unavoidable mess and uncertainty?
Can he retain enjoyment when others control the system design?

biography.name: Sadie Nguyen

background.family: Lives with two parents and an older brother who recently left for college; grandmother visits for several months most years.
background.finances: Comfortable household finances and stable housing; paid enrichment is available but not mandatory.
background.geography: Round Rock, Texas; grandmother lives primarily in southern California.
background.cultureLanguages: English is dominant; understands everyday Vietnamese better than she speaks it.
background.school: Public high school; enjoys biology and history, with grades affected by procrastination more than lack of access.
background.accessOpportunities: Home internet, school laboratories, public health-science events, family travel, and medical follow-up for her own asthma.

timeline.story: At four Sadie liked elaborate pretend restaurants with her brother and insisted that every dish came with a leaf garnish. She wheezed during some colds and received adult-directed care, but most memories from this period involve toys, swimming lessons, and resisting bedtime. Her family did not organize all activities around her health.

At six she asked repeated questions about why breathing sometimes felt tight. A clinician used a simple picture and her parents helped her follow her care plan. Sadie also became intensely interested in medieval castles that year. She remembers both interests as ordinary questions rather than the beginning of a special calling.

At eight she kept a snail briefly in an appropriate container with adult help and watched how it moved toward food. She disliked cleaning the container and returned it outdoors. Her brother called that giving up; she said she had learned what she wanted. They argued and then resumed building a blanket castle together.

At ten she liked a classroom lesson comparing organs across animals and borrowed a book that was too advanced. She skipped most pages and studied diagrams. Her grandmother developed a minor recurring health problem, and Sadie liked explaining familiar diagrams to her, although her grandmother mostly wanted company and a television companion.

At twelve she began following health videos and became annoyed when different presenters sounded equally certain while disagreeing. Her parents helped her distinguish entertainment from information without banning everything. She stopped watching some channels but kept others because the presenters were funny. Her curiosity and her viewing habits did not always match.

At fourteen she attended a supervised science event where students examined prepared slides and practiced basic lab safety. She enjoyed noticing structures but found recording every observation tedious. When her friend fainted during an unrelated school assembly, Sadie called a teacher, stayed out of the way, and felt no wish to become the helper in charge.

Now sixteen she wants to take advanced biology and complete an independent comparison of reliable sources for a school assignment. She enjoys illness mechanisms more than personal symptom conversations. She misses her brother and sometimes delays work to keep chatting with him online. Her future ideas change between weeks, and she does not find that especially alarming.

activities: Calls and games with her brother
Comparing sources for a class project
demonstratedSkills: Identifies when a claim needs checking
ambitions: Take advanced biology
Finish a source-comparison assignment she can defend
practicalConstraints: Asthma care plan affects some activity choices
Advanced equipment available mainly at school

biography.selfDescription: I can be interested in an illness without wanting to hear the entire story of someone’s symptoms at lunch. Maybe that is rude; I try not to say it that way. I like finding out how something works. Then I can get bored with writing it down, which is inconvenient. I do not have a permanent future idea. I have next year’s classes, and I am actually excited about those.
openQuestions: Does interest deepen when recording and repetition become unavoidable?
What will remain appealing beyond accessible explanations and familiar conditions?

biography.name: Jalen Brooks

background.family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; nearby cousins visit most weekends.
background.finances: Stable working household with careful spending and one shared family computer.
background.geography: Garland, Texas; has lived in the same apartment complex since kindergarten.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American family; English at home; family gatherings often center on sports and food.
background.school: Large comprehensive public high school; generally attends, but completes little work in two classes.
background.accessOpportunities: School teams, neighborhood basketball courts, library, reliable phone internet, and parents who can occasionally provide rides.

timeline.story: Jalen spent preschool afternoons in his grandmother's apartment while his parents worked. He liked lining up toy cars by which ones looked fastest, then abandoned the arrangement when cousins arrived. Adults called him sociable because he followed older children everywhere. He was much quieter around unfamiliar adults and often let his cousin answer questions for him.

In first grade he learned to read on schedule but disliked reading aloud when classmates might laugh. Recess mattered more to him than classroom rewards. His father signed him up for basketball, and Jalen enjoyed the uniforms and postgame snacks as much as playing. At home he could spend a whole evening replaying one racing game.

By nine he knew which neighborhood children were good at which games and arranged teams so his friends stayed together. Teachers found him pleasant and easily distracted. He usually finished worksheets if someone sat nearby. He began asking for expensive sneakers after an older cousin explained which brands people noticed, although his parents rarely agreed to buy them.

During remote schooling he kept his camera off and sometimes played games after opening the required assignments. His mother discovered several missing projects late in the semester. The resulting restrictions produced arguments but did not create a lasting homework routine. Online matches became a reliable place to meet friends when visits and basketball practices were interrupted.

Returning to school, Jalen cared intensely about sitting with the right lunch group. He practiced basketball enough to make a school squad but disliked conditioning and eventually stopped trying out. A short relationship conducted mostly through messages ended awkwardly. He deleted photographs together but still checked the girl's posts. His grades varied according to how closely teachers monitored him.

He became the regular organizer of his friends' evening gaming sessions, remembering schedules and settling minor disagreements over team choices. In class, he could explain material verbally and still leave the written assignment blank. His parents argued about whether taking away his console would help. Jalen found their arguments embarrassing and avoided inviting friends over when tensions were high.

At sixteen he works one Saturday shift stocking drinks at an uncle's convenience store, a routine he finds tolerable when the store is quiet. He knows the shelves and notices missing products without prompting. He remains behind in English and chemistry. His closest friend has started making other plans, leaving Jalen unsure how much of their group will last.

motivations: Keeping his place in his friend group
ambitions: Wants a job that pays enough for his own car
Sometimes says he will keep playing competitive games; has no concrete plan
struggles: Attention divided between phone and homework
practicalConstraints: Parents cannot drive him to activities every evening

biography.selfDescription: I'm funny when I know people. Teachers say I could do better, which I already know, so hearing it again doesn't really help. I can remember everything about a game and forget one worksheet. I don't think that means I'm lazy at everything. Mostly I want people to stop asking what I'm going to be, because I don't have an answer that sounds good yet.
openQuestions: Will he accept structured help for the missing coursework?
How much does he enjoy games themselves versus being with the group?
What will he choose if his friends reduce their gaming time?

biography.name: Esmeralda "Esme" Ríos

background.family: Lives with her mother, stepfather, and two younger brothers; father lives in another Texas city and contact is irregular.
background.finances: Family convenience shop provides a variable but usually sufficient income; little money for unpaid programs.
background.geography: Brownsville, Texas; cousins live on both sides of the border.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American; Spanish and English used daily; translates some business correspondence with her mother.
background.school: Public early college high school; passing courses, with stronger applied math than extended essays.
background.accessOpportunities: Frequent access to shop records and customer interactions; school computer lab; limited transport outside the family routine.

timeline.story: Esme learned the route from the family apartment to her grandmother's home before she knew its street name. She liked playing store with empty boxes, but only if someone else pretended to buy something. When adults switched between Spanish and English she usually followed both conversations, occasionally repeating a phrase simply because it sounded funny.

Her parents separated while she was in elementary school. Nobody explained the timetable for visits in a way she could count on, so she stopped packing her overnight bag early. School stayed ordinary and fairly enjoyable. She liked arithmetic pages with clear stopping points and disliked being asked to write about her family for classroom displays.

Her mother began managing a small shop with the man who later became Esme's stepfather. Esme spent afternoons behind the counter doing homework or watching videos. She learned which customers wanted conversation and which wanted their change quickly. She also got bored, complained about the air conditioning, and envied classmates who could go straight home after school.

At ten she began copying invoice totals into a spreadsheet after her mother showed her the steps. She enjoyed making columns line up and finding a duplicated charge. Remote classes later happened in a cramped back room. She could hear customers through the door, and interrupted work often remained unfinished until someone reminded her several times.

Starting an early college program made the adults proud. Esme liked knowing exactly which credits she was earning, although she was not excited by every subject. Her closest friendship cooled after repeated canceled sleepovers. Her brothers needed watching, and her mother treated that arrangement as obvious. Esme argued about it, then usually stayed home anyway.

She took over a weekly stock order draft, comparing what sold with what remained on the shelf. Her stepfather sometimes changed it without explaining why, which she resented. A classmate invited her to join a school business competition; she went to one meeting but could not manage the travel schedule. She has not decided whether to try again.

At sixteen Esme can reconcile a routine day's cash and help compose short supplier emails, though she gets nervous making unfamiliar phone calls. Her mother talks about a prestigious university and a profession with a title. Esme imagines having an office with regular hours and enough privacy to leave work behind. The babysitting arguments continue, especially before exams.

enjoys: Customer gossip when the shop is quiet
avoids: Family discussions that assume she is always available
demonstratedSkills: Switches language for familiar customer needs
unfamiliarActivities: Running a project without adult oversight
ambitions: Wants a regular office job and her own apartment someday
Interested in finishing an associate degree; uncertain about further study
supports: Grandmother provides meals and occasional childcare
practicalConstraints: Cannot assume unpaid opportunities are affordable

biography.selfDescription: People think I like working at the shop because I'm good at some of it. Sometimes I do, especially if I can fix a list and be finished. Sometimes I just want to sit somewhere that doesn't smell like the freezer motor. I don't want every plan to become a family discussion. I also know my mother is tired. Both things are true and we still argue.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy office tasks away from family obligations?
Which responsibilities could realistically be shared?
Does she want more college or mainly want an acceptable way to leave the shop routine?

biography.name: Noor Siddiqui

background.family: Lives with two parents and an older sister who is away at college; family relationships are warm but sometimes overprotective.
background.finances: Comfortable professional household; access to books, devices, and occasional paid classes.
background.geography: Sugar Land, Texas; grandparents live in Houston.
background.cultureLanguages: Pakistani American Muslim family; English dominant, understands conversational Urdu; religious participation varies by activity.
background.school: Homeschooled through middle school, now attends a small secular private high school.
background.accessOpportunities: Parent-supported museum visits, laboratory elective, tutoring, and reliable transportation; independent social experience is relatively recent.

timeline.story: Noor liked pouring water between containers in the kitchen and asking whether the same cup could hold different amounts. Her father answered some questions and told her to stop flooding the counter on other days. She played elaborate pretend restaurant games with her sister. She was comfortable among cousins but watched other preschoolers for a long time before joining them.

Her parents chose homeschooling partly for flexibility around family travel. Noor finished short lessons quickly and spent long afternoons reading whatever was already in the house. A picture book about digestion interested her more than the animal stories beside it. Her mother arranged playdates, usually with the same three families, so Noor rarely had to initiate friendships herself.

She became curious about what bodies did during sleep and why food labels listed different nutrients. At a science museum she repeatedly visited a display with a model heart. She also loved a silly television competition and wanted to be left alone to watch it. Adults sometimes described her as serious when she was simply unsure what to say.

A home experiment growing seeds in different light conditions lasted until the seedlings died during a trip. Noor recorded measurements faithfully at first and then forgot several days. Her sister teased her about calling every notebook a research journal. During remote activities she found text chat easier than video conversation and began sharing pet photographs with another homeschooled child.

She asked to attend a school with laboratory classes because household experiments felt repetitive. Her parents spent a year discussing the change. Meanwhile she worried about looking young beside other girls and copied their clothing choices from social media. A friend who seemed effortlessly confident sometimes left her feeling foolish without doing anything deliberately unkind.

At private school Noor enjoyed preparing microscope slides and comparing different samples. She was less comfortable when partners expected her to improvise a procedure. She learned the cafeteria seating pattern by following a friendly classmate. Her first crush remained mostly a private story told to her sister. Her parents still expected detailed updates whenever an after-school plan changed.

At sixteen she is investigating how different handwashing routines affect safe classroom proxy samples under her teacher's supervision. She likes the repeated observations and dislikes turning them into a polished presentation. She has a dependable lunch group but rarely initiates weekend plans. Her interest in bodily processes is real; her idea of what daily adult work looks like remains quite vague.

demonstratedSkills: Keeps careful observation tables when a routine is established
motivations: Understanding how ordinary bodily processes work
ambitions: Wants further study in something involving living systems
Has no settled job idea
struggles: Confidence drops when procedures are ambiguous

biography.selfDescription: I like finding out what something actually looks like instead of just reading the diagram. I don't think I'm the best science person in my class. Some people answer so quickly. I need a minute, and then usually I have something. I want to be invited places but I also get relieved when plans are canceled. My sister says that is more normal than I think.
openQuestions: How will she respond to investigation with less procedural guidance?
Will her confidence change with greater independent experience?
Which parts of her biology interest last beyond familiar classroom settings?

biography.name: Wyatt Mercer

background.family: Lives with his father and father’s partner; mother lives ninety minutes away, with visits that depend on transport and adults getting along.
background.finances: Household bills are usually paid but work hours fluctuate; two older vehicles require frequent attention.
background.geography: Rural community outside Abilene, Texas; school is a long bus ride away.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking white family; local connections through relatives, work, and hunting-season conversations, though Wyatt rarely hunts.
background.school: Small public high school; repeated absences and a long pattern of incomplete coursework.
background.accessOpportunities: Phone internet and some borrowed tools; few nearby programs, limited rides, and little active adult help navigating options.

timeline.story: Wyatt spent much of his early childhood at his aunt's house with several cousins. He liked cartoons, cereal, and sitting near the adults without being asked questions. He was not especially interested in the toy tractors people bought him because he lived in the country. His favorite activity was making the dog chase a battered tennis ball.

He learned letters more slowly than a cousin of the same age and disliked the comparison. By second grade he could read simple books but rarely chose them. His parents argued about money and household chores. Wyatt preferred sleeping at his aunt's because bedtime there happened at roughly the same time every night, although nobody called it a problem.

After his parents separated, school paperwork and weekend arrangements moved between houses unevenly. He forgot library books and sometimes missed the bus. A teacher let him finish work during lunch, which helped for a while. Outside school he mostly watched videos with cousins. He tried youth baseball for one season and was relieved when it ended.

His father moved farther from town, making visits to friends difficult. Wyatt became good at waiting: in vehicles, outside workplaces, and at the kitchen table while adults decided a plan. Remote schooling supplied very little structure. He logged in inconsistently and passed on a reduced set of work. The gaps remained noticeable when ordinary classes resumed.

He began missing school whenever he had stayed up late and could not face the bus ride. Sometimes he told his father his stomach hurt; sometimes he simply admitted he did not want to go. He liked a history teacher's stories but rarely completed the related assignments. Arguments about attendance became familiar and ended with threats that were inconsistently enforced.

Wyatt's father expected him to help clear scrap and hold parts during vehicle repairs. Wyatt could follow familiar instructions but was not fascinated by engines. He liked watching short comedy clips and playing one phone game. He briefly dated a girl from his bus route; the relationship mostly involved sitting together. Their breakup made the ride uncomfortable for several months.

At sixteen Wyatt is failing two courses and attending an afternoon credit-recovery period when he comes to school. He can work steadily stacking feed bags beside an adult he knows, but avoids asking strangers about openings. His father talks about him joining a relative's crew. Wyatt says maybe because he has not explored anything else and wants the discussion to end.

enjoys: Quiet time with his aunt’s dog
avoids: Long bus days after little sleep
Activities requiring meeting a new group alone
activities: Occasional paid feed-store unloading through a relative
demonstratedSkills: Works steadily on familiar physical routines with clear directions
Notices when a usual supply is missing
unfamiliarActivities: Most clubs and electives outside required subjects
ambitions: Sometimes says he wants to finish school
Has no independently chosen longer-term plan
struggles: Low willingness to start unfamiliar tasks
supports: One school attendance worker checks in

biography.selfDescription: I don't have a secret thing I'm amazing at. I like normal stuff. When somebody asks what my passion is, I just say cars because then they stop asking, but I don't know much about them. School feels like walking into a room where everyone already started. I know missing more makes it worse. Knowing that doesn't make me want to get on the bus tomorrow.
openQuestions: What makes a school day manageable enough for him to attend?
What preferences might appear with low-pressure exposure to unfamiliar activities?
Can adults establish expectations that remain consistent across weeks?

biography.name: Marisol Vega

background.family: Lives with her mother, grandmother, and younger brother; parents separated amicably and father lives nearby.
background.finances: Modest but stable income; several relatives coordinate transport and occasional costs.
background.geography: San Antonio, Texas; extended family concentrated in nearby neighborhoods.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American; English at school, mixed English and Spanish with family; regular large family celebrations.
background.school: Large public high school; average grades and strong attendance; participates in an emergency-response youth program.
background.accessOpportunities: School athletics and a city-supported youth response program; access depends on shared rides and borrowed equipment.

timeline.story: Marisol liked being assigned a job during family gatherings, especially carrying napkins where everyone could see her helping. She also interrupted cousins' games when she thought they were excluding her. Her grandmother kept a predictable afternoon routine of snacks, television, and a walk. Marisol learned the neighbors' names because she liked stopping to talk along the route.

At elementary school she was eager to be line leader and disappointed when she had to wait her turn. Reading came easily enough, while handwriting annoyed her. Her mother enrolled her in a low-cost soccer program. Marisol liked the noisy sideline encouragement and the feeling of belonging to a named team more than practicing alone in the yard.

A firefighter visited her classroom and demonstrated protective equipment. Marisol remembered the radio chatter and the way people checked each other's gear. She did not immediately announce a future occupation. That year she mainly wanted a glittery phone case and permission to stay up for a television finale. Her friendships involved frequent arguments that were forgotten by recess.

During a neighborhood power outage she accompanied her grandmother to check on an older neighbor. She liked having a clear, finite task: carry a charged lantern and bring back the empty one. Later she repeated the story enough that her brother rolled his eyes. At school she struggled with fractions and needed repeated examples before a procedure stuck.

Marisol moved into a larger middle school and became self-conscious about being taller than most friends. Soccer gave her a place where her body felt useful, although she disliked photographs posted after games. She sometimes joined classmates in mocking a girl's awkward messages and felt uncomfortable when adults discussed online kindness. She has never directly repaired that relationship.

A cousin invited her to a youth emergency-response demonstration. Marisol joined the following term, enjoying equipment checks, radio practice, and timed group exercises. She was slower at recalling unfamiliar terminology than some teammates. When nervous, she spoke too quickly over the radio. A patient leader rehearsed with her until she could deliver short messages at a usable pace.

At sixteen she helps prepare practice stations and reliably brings the attendance list. She likes exercises with coordinated roles and an obvious finish. She is less interested in reading lengthy manuals at home. Her mother worries about dangerous work and promotes college programs with predictable hours. Marisol has not decided whether her response interest belongs in her future or just her present weekends.

ambitions: Interested in doing something active with a dependable team
Also wants college because her mother considers it essential
practicalConstraints: Time split with soccer and family

biography.selfDescription: I like when everybody knows what they're doing and you can tell if the team got it done. I'm not the person who remembers every big word first. I can practice something a lot without getting tired of it, though. People say I'm confident because I'm loud. Sometimes I'm loud because I don't know what else to do. I still want my friends to think I'm fun.
openQuestions: Will she sustain interest when activities involve more study and less group excitement?
How does she respond to a role without visible recognition?
Can she address the unresolved harm in her former peer group?

biography.name: Theo Chen

background.family: Lives with two mothers and an older half-brother who visits during college breaks; family accepts his identity and argues about ordinary household responsibilities.
background.finances: Stable middle-income household; purchases usually require saving or choosing between alternatives.
background.geography: Richardson, Texas; moved from Seattle at age eight.
background.cultureLanguages: Chinese American and white mixed family; English dominant, limited Mandarin with one grandparent; transgender boy.
background.school: Public high school with a technical elective sequence; strong computing work, uneven humanities grades.
background.accessOpportunities: A refurbished laptop, school electronics bench, library makerspace, and parents able to provide some transport.

timeline.story: Theo liked assembling the same train track around the living-room table and became annoyed when someone improved it without asking. He could also spend an hour narrating imaginary arguments between plastic animals. His mothers noticed that he preferred a small number of familiar playmates. At preschool he often watched group games until the rules were obvious before participating.

An older neighbor let him press buttons on a broken radio while explaining what each knob used to do. Theo liked opening the case more than listening to the explanation. His family kept a box of safe discarded components for him. Many projects amounted to arranging pieces on the floor and declaring them an invention, with no working mechanism.

Moving to Texas interrupted his friendships. He stayed in contact with one friend through a building game and learned to troubleshoot their connection problems by trying settings one at a time. He was confident on that familiar screen and reluctant to introduce himself at school. His mothers enrolled him in a camp he found too noisy and socially exhausting.

He began modifying small game scripts after following online examples. He often copied code he did not understand and became angry when a tiny change broke it. A library volunteer showed him how to test one change before adding another. He still preferred a working result to explanations. Outside computing he mostly read comics and avoided the family hiking plans.

Theo asked his family and school to use his current name. His mothers handled paperwork and practical questions, while a few classmates made the transition socially awkward. He remained preoccupied with the same games and projects. His closest friendship deepened through ordinary shared lunches, complaints about homework, and arguments about which online videos were actually funny.

An electronics elective gave him access to a breadboard and inexpensive sensors. He built a temperature display, then spent weeks making its case look less lopsided. He could explain the code to his teacher but froze when classmates gathered to watch. His brother called him a genius jokingly, a compliment Theo disliked because he knew how much he had copied and retried.

At sixteen he maintains a small game server for five friends and fixes routine problems reliably. He has not built a large application and loses interest in abstract coding exercises without a purpose he cares about. He is behind in an English project and keeps postponing a meeting about it. At home, abandoned components on the dining table cause recurring arguments.

enjoys: Small electronics that produce visible output
demonstratedSkills: Tests code changes systematically when he slows down
Builds simple circuits from documented examples
ambitions: Wants more time and equipment for projects
Thinks further technical study might suit him but has not compared options

biography.selfDescription: I know things about a couple of games and some very specific hardware. That doesn't mean I know all computers. I get annoyed when people hand me a random broken phone. I like solving my own problem, but sometimes I just want to play. I'd rather show someone a thing after it works. If they stand behind me while I try, I forget everything.
openQuestions: Will technical interest extend beyond self-selected projects?
What group size and working conditions support his confidence?
Can he maintain necessary coursework without every assignment needing a personal application?

biography.name: Kayla Washington

background.family: Lives with her mother and younger sister; father lives in Louisiana and calls most weeks; mother and daughter have ongoing disagreements about grades and appearances.
background.finances: Stable but closely budgeted household; mother works changing hospital shifts.
background.geography: Pearland, Texas; frequent summer visits to relatives in Louisiana.
background.cultureLanguages: Black American; English at home; church attendance mainly with grandmother during visits.
background.school: Large public high school; biology grades strong, other grades fluctuate with missing work.
background.accessOpportunities: School laboratory classes, phone internet, beauty-store browsing, and occasional library events; after-school transport inconsistent.

timeline.story: Kayla liked choosing outfits for herself and her sister, though her sister rarely cooperated. She asked her mother why bandages stuck to skin and why scabs changed color. Her mother answered what she could after work. Kayla also enjoyed pretend cooking and long stretches of cartoons, with no particular sign that any one interest would dominate later.

She liked school when teachers used pictures and demonstrations. Spelling practice bored her, and she negotiated for shorter sessions at the kitchen table. A cousin let her help braid a doll's hair, beginning an interest in styles and products. She sometimes wanted to cut her own hair after a bad day, but her mother insisted they wait until the weekend.

At nine she received permission to watch selected hair-care videos. She became fascinated by why one product left flakes and another did not. Her experiments were informal mixtures in cups that her mother eventually banned from the bathroom sink. A close friendship ended when the other child moved; Kayla acted indifferent but continued asking relatives whether their family might move back.

During remote classes Kayla followed beauty creators and fitness accounts with increasing attention. She compared her face with filtered images without always remembering the filters. Her mother criticized the amount of time she spent looking at herself, which made Kayla more secretive. She completed some science activities eagerly and ignored assignments she thought no adult would actually check.

Puberty made her curious about skin, sweat, and menstrual cycles, partly because classroom explanations seemed too brief. She read product labels and asked a pharmacist a question with her mother nearby. She also believed several confident online claims before a science teacher helped her compare their evidence. She did not become uniformly skeptical; attractive videos still persuaded her quickly.

Kayla liked biology practicals involving magnification and observable change. She disliked memorizing lists for tests and earned lower marks than she expected. She began posting short hairstyle clips, deleting any that received few reactions. A friendship became strained when a friend posted an unflattering photograph. Her mother dismissed the argument as childish, and they stopped discussing that group in detail.

At sixteen she can follow a classroom investigation, record observations, and explain why a comparison needs similar starting conditions. She enjoys the questions more than long reports. She still sometimes stays home after a sleepless night spent messaging and scrolling. Her mother promotes a respected health-related degree; Kayla likes parts of the subject but is uncertain about committing years to it.

enjoys: Questions about skin and bodily changes
avoids: Conversations that turn immediately into criticism
activities: Helping sister get ready for school
demonstratedSkills: Notices differences in texture and appearance
motivations: Understanding changes in her own body
ambitions: Interested in further study related to bodies or products
Sometimes imagines building a popular account but has no stable plan
supports: Mother provides practical care despite conflict
practicalConstraints: No regular ride to evening activities

biography.selfDescription: I ask questions because I actually want to know, not because I already decided to do that for work. My mom hears one thing about biology and starts talking about degrees. Sometimes I like making a video more than doing anything for school. Then somebody comments and I hate the whole app. I can tell a friend not to compare herself and still do it myself five minutes later.
openQuestions: Which scientific questions sustain her attention away from appearance concerns?
How much does she enjoy making content when reactions are hidden?
Can she and her mother discuss options without treating curiosity as commitment?

biography.name: Luis Alberto Peña

background.family: Lives with his father, stepmother, and infant half-sister; his mother lives in El Paso and communicates by phone; persistent tension with father.
background.finances: Rent and food covered through two hourly incomes; little cushion for lost shifts or major repairs.
background.geography: Fort Worth, Texas; moved from El Paso at eleven.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican American; bilingual Spanish and English; follows both English- and Spanish-language football coverage.
background.school: Public high school; enrolled in a basic business applications course; often late and academically disengaged.
background.accessOpportunities: School computer access and a family-connected weekend job; limited encouragement to try extracurricular activities.

timeline.story: Luis lived with his mother and grandmother for most of his preschool years while his father worked elsewhere. He liked being allowed to sort coins into an old muffin tin. Usually he wanted cartoons or someone to kick a ball with him. His grandmother described him as easy because he did not ask for many outings or new toys.

His parents briefly lived together again when he started school. Luis liked his teacher's strict schedule and knew which task came after lunch. At home plans changed more often. He began watching football with his father, learning player names and arguing about results. He was not especially keen to join a team, despite adults assuming that watching meant wanting to play.

He spent afternoons with two boys from his building, mostly trading video clips and playing a simple console game. School reports called him capable but inconsistent. He could finish arithmetic quickly and leave a whole writing page empty. His father thought longer homework hours would fix this. Luis sat at the table longer without necessarily producing more work.

A move to Fort Worth followed his parents' final separation. Luis missed his grandmother's apartment and stopped expecting weekend plans with old friends to happen. He entered a new school halfway through the year and mostly kept to himself. Remote learning soon afterward made it easy to disappear into the background while claiming that he had completed everything required.
