biography.selfDescription: I liked the science fair most when somebody stopped looking puzzled. I want to understand what is happening in a pond, and I also want to find a good way to show it without pretending one interest cancels the other.
openQuestions: Will laboratory routines appeal as much as field observations?
How does she respond to extended creative critique?

biography.name: Alex

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sister.
background.finances: Stable moderate income; future transport and housing would require budgeting.
background.geography: Arlington, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English at home; extended family meets for game nights.
background.school: Public high school with computer classes and a club website project.
background.accessOpportunities: Tutorials, school computers, and two classmates willing to test a small site.

timeline.story: In 2014, Alex liked building long tracks for marbles and changing the sections where they stopped. He also enjoyed board games with relatives, particularly the moment everyone understood a rule that had initially seemed confusing.

At six, he began using a classroom tablet and wondered why some buttons did nothing. During 2017, he made paper menus for pretend games but cared more about whether the choices worked than how the menus looked.

In 2018, Alex tried a school presentation and disliked standing in front of the room. He was more comfortable discussing a problem at a table, where others could point to the same object instead of watching only him.

During 2020, he followed beginner tutorials and experimented with simple web pages. Many attempts failed, and he learned to make one small change before checking the result rather than replacing several lines at once.

At twelve, Alex helped a school club put basic information online. In 2023, he kept a bug list after two classmates tried the site and found problems he had missed because he already knew how it was supposed to work.

Across 2024 and 2025, Alex revised the small site and practiced explaining navigation. Comfortable school mathematics helped, but large software systems remained unfamiliar; performing art and managing retail sales held little appeal compared with focused building and occasional team discussion.

At sixteen in 2026, Alex is exploring Texas college computing courses and short workshops. He imagines a modest place and reliable transport, while wanting to learn whether he enjoys unfamiliar programming tasks as much as improving the club site he understands well.

ambitions: Explore college computing and practical workshops
He imagines a modest independent home, reliable transport, and time with a small circle of friends.
struggles: Can keep polishing a familiar feature

biography.selfDescription: I like when a bug becomes something I can explain and fix instead of something mysterious. Talking with users helps, but the part I look forward to is sitting down and making the site work better.
openQuestions: Does interest generalize to unfamiliar systems?
How will he respond to longer projects with less visible progress?

biography.name: Drew

background.family: Lives with their mother and grandmother.
background.finances: Modest but steady income; savings and dependable work matter.
background.geography: Temple, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; extended family frequently asks for help with devices.
background.school: Public high school without a coding course that fits their schedule.
background.accessOpportunities: Library instructions, family devices, and school career advising.

timeline.story: In 2014, Drew enjoyed matching objects to pictures and helping sort kitchen utensils. They liked knowing where things belonged, but also invented sprawling games in which the utensils became vehicles and lost all resemblance to their original purpose.

At six, they began helping a grandparent find familiar television settings. During 2017, Drew learned that trying the same button repeatedly was less useful than remembering what changed after each attempt and asking before changing an unfamiliar setting.

In 2018, Drew liked school science demonstrations when instructions were clear. Mathematics felt comfortable some weeks and difficult others, and comments about naturally gifted classmates made them wonder whether technical interests required a special kind of brilliance.

During 2020, relatives asked Drew to help reconnect devices during online calls. They followed instructions, tested one possible fix at a time, and felt pleased when someone could join the conversation without needing to replace the device.

At twelve, Drew started writing simple notes about successful fixes. In 2023, they explained a connection problem patiently to a relative but still asked an adult to check unfamiliar instructions before attempting changes beyond their experience.

Across 2024 and 2025, Drew remained interested in practical computer support without access to coding classes. They often described new tools as things requiring help, while a teacher encouraged them to separate needing instruction from assuming they could never learn.

At sixteen in 2026, Drew is comparing Texas certificates and college options for practical technology study. They want useful service and steady income, with no assumption that research is the destination or that their worries constitute a diagnosed condition.

avoids: Being told only geniuses can work with technology
demonstratedSkills: Tests one change at a time
ambitions: Compare certificates and college introductions
They imagine a dependable home, growing savings, and ordinary independence near people they trust.

biography.selfDescription: I do not feel like a computer expert, but I like figuring out one small problem at a time. I would rather ask for help and understand what changed than pretend I knew the answer from the start.
openQuestions: What confidence changes after structured introductory training?
Which mathematical demands actually appear in routes they explore?

biography.name: Casey

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sister.
background.finances: Stable middle income; family discusses saving and predictable bills.
background.geography: Waco, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with regular extended-family gatherings.
background.school: Public high school with spreadsheets in a business elective.
background.accessOpportunities: Club receipts and adult review; no professional financial responsibility.

timeline.story: In 2014, Casey enjoyed playing shop with cousins but preferred sorting the pretend coins to persuading anyone to buy something. She also liked painting large, messy pictures that bore little resemblance to her orderly game materials.

At six, she began tracking library books on a homemade list. During 2017, a missing entry caused an argument with her sister, and she learned that having a neat chart did not guarantee its information was complete.

In 2018, Casey helped plan a small class celebration and liked checking whether the available money covered the supplies. She disliked the fundraising pitch, especially being asked to make classmates feel guilty for not contributing.

During 2020, she learned basic spreadsheets for school and began comparing planned with actual household project costs when parents invited her. She enjoyed explaining differences without being responsible for adults’ bills or financial decisions.

At twelve, Casey volunteered to help with a club budget. In 2023, several receipts did not match the recorded balance, and she worked with an adult to locate duplicate entries rather than assuming someone had taken money.

Across 2024 and 2025, she reconciled more club receipts under review and learned to explain why a balance changed. Exciting investment stories interested her less than reliable records, and sales targets sounded stressful rather than motivating.

At sixteen in 2026, Casey is comparing Texas accounting degrees and bookkeeping study. She values predictable work and savings, while recognizing that school records have taught her nothing about preparing audited accounts, advising clients, or meeting professional financial responsibilities.

ambitions: Compare accounting and bookkeeping routes
She imagines a steady routine, manageable expenses, and time with friends without financial drama.

biography.selfDescription: I like finding the ordinary reason a number changed. A balanced club sheet is satisfying, but I know that is a small setting and I still need to see what the everyday work looks like somewhere larger.
openQuestions: Would professional repetition remain satisfying?
How would deadlines and consequential errors affect her enjoyment?

biography.name: Morgan

background.family: Lives with his father and stepmother; younger sibling shares the home.
background.finances: Moderate income; long professional study would need cost planning.
background.geography: Dallas, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family enjoys discussing local news with differing opinions.
background.school: Public high school with debate and research assignments.
background.accessOpportunities: Library databases and teacher feedback; no legal practice exposure.

timeline.story: In 2014, Morgan liked retelling stories from the viewpoint of whichever character had been blamed. He also built block forts and occasionally changed the rules of entry so often that cousins refused to keep playing.

At six, he became interested in classroom rules and asked why exceptions existed. During 2017, a teacher helped him understand that a fair rule might still need different support for children starting in different circumstances.

In 2018, Morgan enjoyed comparing two accounts of the same historical event. He initially treated disagreement as proof someone was lying, then learned that perspective and incomplete information could produce different accounts without deliberate deception.

During 2020, he read widely and argued about news at home. His stepmother asked him to summarize the other person’s view before replying, a practice he found irritating but later useful in school discussions.

At twelve, Morgan joined debate and liked weighing evidence more than memorizing a dramatic opening. In 2023, he researched competing accounts for a school argument and discovered that one attractive claim rested on a weak source.

Across 2024 and 2025, he revised written arguments after feedback and became more comfortable speaking to classmates. Explaining rules and rights appealed more than selling products, while he knew little about the paperwork and responsibilities of actual legal work.

At sixteen in 2026, Morgan is comparing Texas college pathways, possible professional study, and paralegal work. He imagines a future home and occasional travel, but wants to see ordinary legal workplaces before assuming debate enjoyment predicts satisfaction or readiness.

ambitions: Compare professional study and paralegal work
He imagines a settled home, close friendships, and occasional travel alongside useful work.

biography.selfDescription: I like an argument more when I have to take the other account seriously. Debate has made me curious about law, but I have not seen enough ordinary legal work to know whether the daily responsibilities would suit me.
openQuestions: Would detailed case administration interest him?
How would he respond when advocacy requires representing a view he dislikes?

biography.name: Ash

background.family: Lives with his mother, stepfather, and younger sibling.
background.finances: Modest stable income; paid learning has practical appeal.
background.geography: Garland, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with relatives working in varied occupations.
background.school: Public high school with supervised low-voltage classroom kits.
background.accessOpportunities: School diagrams and adult-guided household measuring; no electrical installation experience.

timeline.story: In 2014, Ash enjoyed assembling toy tracks and making sure every piece connected before starting a race. He also liked drawing imaginary animals, rarely feeling any need to make their parts fit a believable explanation.

At six, he began helping a parent measure shelves before buying storage boxes. During 2017, he learned that a small measuring error could matter even when an object looked approximately right from across the room.

In 2018, Ash joined a school craft group and liked projects with understandable diagrams. He became frustrated by instructions that omitted a step, then learned to compare the picture with the parts before deciding the whole project was impossible.

During 2020, he completed practical school assignments at home with adult help where needed. He liked having a clear sequence and a partner to ask, but sometimes avoided starting when he was unsure which materials could be used safely.

At twelve, Ash encountered a low-voltage circuit kit in class. In 2023, he enjoyed following its diagram and tracing a loose connection, finding that a small, carefully checked change restored the behavior the instructions described.

Across 2024 and 2025, Ash completed supervised kit exercises and helped measure parts for a household project. Paid apprenticeship learning began to sound attractive, while he recognized that actual electrical installation remained entirely unfamiliar and required appropriate training.

At sixteen in 2026, Ash is comparing Texas apprenticeship information, technical courses, and possible college study. He wants practical teamwork, a dependable car, and growing savings, without assuming a school kit establishes readiness for independent electrical work.

ambitions: Compare paid training with college options
He imagines a dependable car, growing savings, and a steady home life with people he knows well.
struggles: Hesitates when safety boundaries are unclear

biography.selfDescription: I like being able to trace what connects to what. Paid learning sounds good to me, but I still want someone qualified to show me what the real work involves before I decide that the classroom version tells the whole story.
openQuestions: How does he respond to actual workplace schedules?
Which training route provides the support and breadth he wants?

biography.name: Rowan

background.family: Lives with parents and an older sibling.
background.finances: Moderate income; occasional clothing purchases are planned.
background.geography: El Paso, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Spanish within the family.
background.school: Public high school with art and career exploration events.
background.accessOpportunities: Style sketches and one supervised mannequin demonstration; no paid services.

timeline.story: In 2014, Rowan liked dressing paper figures and inventing where each was going that day. They also enjoyed large outdoor games, often changing clothes in the story more frequently than changing the actual game they played.

At six, they began drawing family members in imagined outfits. During 2017, a cousin pointed out that a favorite sketch did not resemble what the cousin wanted, teaching Rowan to ask before assuming a personal preference was universal.

In 2018, Rowan joined a school art group and enjoyed planning colors and shapes. Science experiments and keeping office-style lists held less interest, although they completed the required assignments and occasionally liked an unexpected topic.

During 2020, Rowan collected hairstyle references and sketched possibilities for fictional characters. They enjoyed listening when relatives described what felt comfortable, learning that a style could look appealing in a picture and still fail someone’s everyday routine.

At twelve, Rowan began asking more specific questions before sketching a style for someone. In 2023, a school exploration event introduced the idea of licensed salon training, which sounded worth investigating rather than like a settled decision.

Across 2024 and 2025, Rowan tried a careful technique on a mannequin under supervision and helped organize demonstration tools. They enjoyed the welcoming setting but had never provided a paid salon service or learned how demanding customer situations were handled.

At sixteen in 2026, Rowan is comparing Texas licensed training information and introductory visits. They like spending some money on clothing, but want a realistic view of customer work, practice requirements, and the difference between visual interest and a longer training commitment.

avoids: Science experiments as a main activity
ambitions: Explore licensed training and customer settings
They imagine a friendly adult routine with a comfortable home, personal style, and close social connections.
struggles: May assume a welcoming event reflects all workdays

biography.selfDescription: I like hearing what somebody actually wants before I start drawing an idea. The demonstration was interesting, but a mannequin does not ask difficult questions or have a long day, so I know I still have a lot to see.
openQuestions: How does interest change with repetitive technical practice?
Would sustained customer interaction feel energizing or tiring?

biography.name: Parker

background.family: Lives with his father and grandmother.
background.finances: Modest stable income; paid learning and shared future rent appeal.
background.geography: Killeen, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family shares practical help with neighbors.
background.school: Public high school with a school-event supply room.
background.accessOpportunities: Adult-supervised stock routines; no industrial equipment exposure.

timeline.story: In 2014, Parker liked sorting blocks by shape and then ignoring the categories to build imaginary animals. He enjoyed putting everything away when there was a clear place for it, but resisted adults reorganizing the same shelves without explanation.

At six, he helped a teacher count shared game pieces. During 2017, he noticed that missing pieces often turned up in the wrong box rather than being lost, and suggested putting a picture label on each container.

In 2018, Parker tried a school art activity and enjoyed it without wanting to continue after the project ended. He was more interested in helping set up equipment for the next class than in choosing another elaborate personal creation.

During 2020, he helped keep household supplies organized and used lists for online school tasks. Predictable routines were reassuring, although he still liked casual outdoor play and did not want every free afternoon planned in advance.

At twelve, Parker began volunteering with school-event supplies. In 2023, he learned to check a list before moving materials and to ask an adult about weight, access, or storage rules rather than guessing what could be handled safely.

Across 2024 and 2025, he continued counts, labels, and supervised setup. Satisfaction came from the team finding what it needed, even when no dramatic creative project resulted, and he began asking what paid training might involve in similar settings.

At sixteen in 2026, Parker is comparing Texas practical training introductions. He imagines shared rent and keeping the car already available to him, while recognizing that school routines reveal nothing about industrial machinery, forklift operation, or the demands of a full shift.

avoids: Being pushed to invent a dramatic project
motivations: A team finding what it needs
ambitions: Explore paid practical training
He imagines shared rent, dependable transport, and a steady routine with time for friends.
struggles: Uncertain how full shifts would feel

biography.selfDescription: I like when people can find what they need and get on with their part. It does not have to look exciting to be satisfying, but I still need to find out how a real workday compares with helping at school.
openQuestions: Which routine tasks stay satisfying over a full day?
What physical and scheduling demands are realistic?

biography.name: Remy

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger sibling in a familiar neighborhood.
background.finances: Modest stable income; staying near home currently feels practical.
background.geography: Temple, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking household with extended family nearby.
background.school: Public high school with general courses; no club or job history specified.
background.accessOpportunities: Ordinary school tasks; supportive introductions to new settings are possible.

timeline.story: In 2014, Remy played ordinary household games, sometimes following a sibling’s plan and sometimes making up their own. No single activity occupied most afternoons, and family memories do not identify an early specialist interest.

At six, they began school and enjoyed some days more than others. During 2017, they tried the activities available in class without deciding that any one task described them especially well or needed to continue at home.

In 2018, Remy completed ordinary reading, drawing, mathematics, and group assignments. Some were easier to start than others, but they did not build a distinctive project history, and adults generally accepted that preferences could remain unsettled.

During 2020, they followed the household’s changing school routine with help when needed. Familiar people mattered, while many descriptions of adult work still sounded abstract because Remy had not visited the settings or seen the everyday tasks involved.

At twelve, Remy found it difficult to answer questions about future plans beyond saying they might stay nearby. In 2023, they continued regular classes without joining a club, starting paid work, or arranging a shadowing experience.

Across 2024 and 2025, classmates became more definite about their plans, but Remy still could not picture most activities well enough to judge them. Several new settings sounded worth seeing, without prompting a particular creative project or professional identity.

At sixteen in 2026, Remy wants supportive introductions to Texas college and training settings and time to revisit first impressions. A close-to-home future with low spending is only an initial sketch; uncertainty currently describes missing experience rather than a conclusion about capacity.

avoids: Making a confident claim without experience
demonstratedSkills: Participates in familiar assignments; no specialist skill is assumed
ambitions: Try supportive introductions without choosing a profession
They currently imagine a low-spending life near home, while treating that picture as provisional.
struggles: Comparison pressure from more definite peers

biography.selfDescription: I do not know yet, and I would rather say that than pick something because it sounds like an answer. Seeing a place and having somebody explain an ordinary day might help me work out what I actually think.
openQuestions: Which experiences become meaningful after an introduction?
Will proximity to home remain a preference after broader exposure?

biography.name: Elias Moreno

background.family: Lives with his father and aunt; cousins visit most weekends.
background.finances: Father’s utility job covers essentials; larger purchases require saving.
background.geography: Small town outside San Angelo, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English and conversational Spanish; extended family gatherings feature regional music.
background.school: Small public high school with a shared agricultural shop.
background.accessOpportunities: School bus and library internet; limited local clubs outside athletics.

timeline.story: In 2014, Elias followed his aunt through grocery shopping and asked why identical cans cost different amounts. At home he sorted bottle caps into elaborate arrangements that he changed whenever someone guessed the rule.

In 2016, he joined a children’s dance group with cousins. He remembered sequences easily but disliked the stiff performance clothes. His father built a backyard shade frame, and Elias wanted to help measure everything.
At eight in 2018, he began making detailed maps for imaginary bus routes. A teacher let him explain one to the class; he enjoyed questions about the route more than displaying the drawing itself.

In 2020, unreliable home internet made remote lessons frustrating. His aunt printed assignments at work, and Elias completed them at the kitchen table while helping a cousin invent indoor obstacle courses between video calls.

At twelve, he tried school football because practice provided a late bus. By 2023 he preferred maintaining equipment and keeping statistics, though he still liked the feeling of being part of the sideline group.

During 2024, Elias began earning weekend money stocking a feed store. He learned product locations and asked customers how they used unfamiliar supplies. In 2025 he also started writing short comic scenes with a friend.

In 2026, he is saving for a used laptop and exploring an open house at a Texas technical college. He also wants to see a college theater rehearsal, something he has never watched beyond school productions. He recently asked the librarian to help compare workshop dates before mentioning the idea at home.

ambitions: Spend a summer in a larger city
Find a program with both practical and creative options
He imagines living independently within visiting distance of family, with a useful workshop and friends who make him laugh.
struggles: Quiet when adults assume his interests

biography.selfDescription: I like asking what happens behind the scenes. People remember that I help with football and assume I want everything to involve sports, but I also spend a lot of time writing ridiculous conversations.
openQuestions: Would a larger setting feel freeing or exhausting?
Does he prefer stock work itself or the knowledgeable conversations around it?

biography.name: Caleb Whitlock

background.family: Lives with grandparents; parents remain in contact but do not provide daily care.
background.finances: Grandparents own their home and live on fixed retirement income.
background.geography: Rural East Texas outside Nacogdoches.
background.cultureLanguages: English; family attends a small church, though Caleb is undecided about participation.
background.school: Small public school with mixed-grade electives.
background.accessOpportunities: Workshop at home; long drives to specialized courses.

timeline.story: In 2014, Caleb helped his grandmother sort donated books and mostly chose the ones with maps. His grandfather showed him how to sand wood scraps, but insisted that sharp tools were for later years.

At six, he moved permanently into his grandparents’ home after several changes in his parents’ housing. In 2017, predictable breakfasts and the same school bus stop became reassuring parts of an otherwise confusing period.

In 2018, Caleb joined a children’s choir and surprised himself by enjoying performance. He also collected beetles in temporary jars, releasing them after drawing their legs and arguing with a cousin about whether insects slept.

During 2020, his grandparents kept strict household routines. Caleb learned to email photographs of homework from a phone and listened to long radio programs while making small wooden boxes with increasingly complicated internal dividers.
At twelve, he grew self-conscious about choir and stopped attending for a term. A teacher invited him to read a character in a class play, and by 2023 he was singing again with two friends.

In 2024, Caleb sold several handmade boxes at a community sale, then decided he disliked fulfilling identical orders. In 2025, he spent more time learning bird calls and helping repaint the church’s stage scenery.

At sixteen in 2026, Caleb is considering a Texas community-college woodworking demonstration and a university natural-history event. He wants more independence, but worries that moving away would leave his grandparents with too many household tasks. He recently borrowed a field guide and found several of his confident bird identifications were mistaken.

avoids: Questions about parental history from acquaintances
ambitions: Visit a city independently
Learn techniques beyond home tools
He imagines keeping ties to a quiet place while having enough independence to travel and make things on his own terms.

biography.selfDescription: I enjoy living somewhere quiet, but I do wonder what I am missing. Making one good box is satisfying; making twenty just because someone will buy them sounds much less interesting to me.
openQuestions: Does his reluctance to leave reflect preference or obligation?
Would selling varied work feel different from repeat orders?

biography.name: Zara Hassan

background.family: Lives with her mother, father, and younger brother; extended family is nearby.
background.finances: Moderate income; one parent recently returned to part-time work.
background.geography: Katy, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: English and Arabic; Muslim household with room for individual preferences.
background.school: Public high school; treated for major depressive disorder since fifteen.
background.accessOpportunities: Regular therapy, medical follow-up, school workload adjustments, and family support.

timeline.story: In 2014, Zara liked dancing in the living room and making labels for household drawers. She changed the labels frequently, asking adults whether a different word would make it easier to find what they needed.

At six, she joined a children’s science club and particularly enjoyed experiments involving sound. During 2017, she also learned simple embroidery from an aunt, taking pride in choosing colors nobody else would have paired.

In 2018, Zara became absorbed in detective stories and wrote short mysteries with her brother. She enjoyed planting clues but often wrote endings in which the characters negotiated rather than identifying a single obvious villain.

During 2020, she stayed connected to friends through a shared drawing game and helped organize household meal plans. Some schoolwork felt repetitive, but she kept enjoying small experiments and long conversations with one close friend.

At twelve, she joined a school environmental group and helped map shade around the campus. By 2023, she was still active but increasingly bothered by the gap between the group’s ambitious posters and its limited practical follow-through.

In 2025, persistent low mood, fatigue, and loss of enjoyment led to a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Treatment and reduced commitments helped her return gradually to regular classes and occasional embroidery nights with her aunt.

At sixteen in 2026, Zara attends school consistently and is rebuilding activities cautiously. She is curious about a nearby Texas college’s summer workshop but wants a manageable trial, and she is uncertain which interests will feel meaningful as her energy improves.

avoids: Pressure to describe recovery as a straight line
ambitions: Try one manageable workshop
She imagines a steady adult routine with trusted people and enough energy left for personal projects.

biography.selfDescription: I am interested in things again, but I do not want to promise a giant new version of myself. Sometimes making one small thing with good colors is enough to remind me that I still have preferences.
openQuestions: Which former interests will return, change, or fall away?
How much activity supports recovery without exhausting her?

biography.name: Jonah Landry

background.family: Lives with mother and younger sister near an aunt; parents separated amicably before the move.
background.finances: Hourly income covers essentials with little cushion after replacing belongings lost in a storm.
background.geography: San Antonio, Texas, following hurricane displacement from coastal Louisiana at eleven.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking with Louisiana Creole relatives; recipes and stories connect the family to its old neighborhood.
background.school: Public high school; changed schools twice during relocation.
background.accessOpportunities: Library computers, a bus pass, and used art supplies from a former neighbor support exploration.

timeline.story: Jonah helped an elderly neighbor water porch plants in mismatched containers. He remembered which leaves drooped first and talked about imaginary cities where every roof had a garden that people reached by ladders.

He drew treasure-hunt maps for classmates at recess. His teacher noticed that he revised confusing directions after watching younger children get lost, rather than insisting they should simply have understood his first drawing.

Weekends with his father involved cards and simple recipes. Jonah disliked competitive sports teasing but happily kept score, especially when adults let him design a clearer score sheet with space for everyone’s name.

A hurricane damaged the family’s rental home when he was eleven. They stayed with relatives before moving to Texas; missing possessions bothered him, but losing familiar routes and classmates took longer to explain.
At a new school he stayed quiet until an art teacher asked him to label a hallway display. Making signs gave classmates a reason to talk without asking him to retell the storm story.

He began riding buses independently and sketching intersections while waiting. A community garden volunteer welcomed his idea for clearer watering labels, and Jonah helped test them with people who spoke several different first languages.

He contributes garden instructions and works occasional grocery shifts. He misses the coast without wanting to return immediately, and considers Texas community colleges while wondering whether a residential campus might finally feel like a chosen move. One coworker now trades sketchbook recommendations with him, and Jonah values a friendship that began with ordinary shared shifts rather than explanations.

ambitions: Curious about images and places
Imagines a stable home he chooses, with room for plants and visiting relatives.

biography.selfDescription: I can miss where we lived and still like parts of living here. I notice confusing signs everywhere, probably because I've spent so much time figuring out places that other people already know.
openQuestions: How does stability affect education choices?
Would he draw when nobody needs directions?

biography.name: Zoe Min Park

background.family: Lives with parents and a younger brother; family members learned basic signing after her hearing loss was identified.
background.finances: Comfortable middle income; hearing technology expenses are planned and sometimes delay holidays.
background.geography: Pearland, Texas, with relatives elsewhere in the Houston area.
background.cultureLanguages: Korean American household using English, Korean with grandparents, and some ASL; she chooses among spoken and signed communication by situation.
background.school: Public high school; bilateral moderate hearing loss accommodated with hearing aids, captions, a remote microphone, and seating choices.
background.accessOpportunities: Has accessible art classes and a regional deaf and hard-of-hearing youth group; some extracurricular spaces remain acoustically difficult.

timeline.story: Zoe loved helping decorate birthday cakes with uneven stars and carefully chosen colors. Hearing aids were already part of her routine, but she most often described herself as the person who got to choose the sprinkles.

Her first classroom microphone made lessons easier to follow, while noisy lunch tables remained tiring. One friend began meeting her outside after eating, and they invented sidewalk-chalk games that did not require rapid group conversation.

She joined a youth group where several communication styles were normal. Seeing older teenagers ask confidently for captions gave her language for requests she had previously left her parents to make on her behalf.

During remote school she appreciated captions but disliked being expected to watch faces and worksheets simultaneously. Baking with her brother became a welcome activity where written recipes, gestures, and familiar routines worked together.

She entered a school art show with a series of tiny cake drawings. Praise interested her, yet she also enjoyed calculating how much frosting a real version would need and testing whether colors survived refrigeration.

Zoe tried student council and discovered that meetings could be accessible when agendas arrived beforehand. She helped organize a quiet study night but declined one loud dance committee, explaining her reasons without withdrawing from everything else.

She now bakes for family events, paints, and attends selected council meetings. She is considering Texas postsecondary options with attention to classroom access, but also wants ordinary details—friendly common spaces, useful kitchens, and people who remember to face her.

ambitions: Interested in continuing education
Imagines a home where friends gather around food and communication access is routine.

biography.selfDescription: I like a room where people can hear themselves think, but I don't want a small life. Sometimes I'm quiet because I'm tired of listening, and sometimes I'm just deciding what color the cake should be.
openQuestions: Is event organization enjoyable beyond familiar groups?
Which campus environments reduce fatigue without limiting opportunities?

biography.name: Wyatt Sloane

background.family: Lives with parents and an older brother on a large property; family dinners are regular and disagreements tend to stay mild.
background.finances: Wealth from a family-owned distribution business; college tuition and travel are affordable.
background.geography: Outside Fredericksburg, Texas, with long drives to specialized activities.
background.cultureLanguages: White, English-speaking family with several generations in the Hill Country; church attendance is occasional.
background.school: Small private school; good classroom support but few electives and a fairly uniform peer group.
background.accessOpportunities: Has abundant material resources but low exposure to unfamiliar work, communities, or independent responsibility.

timeline.story: Wyatt liked following the groundskeeper as he checked irrigation and collected fallen branches. He asked many questions but preferred inventing stories about the broken branches to helping carry an entire load to the trailer.

His parents tried horseback riding lessons and tennis. He enjoyed being outdoors but disliked correction in front of other children, so both activities ended before he had enough practice to feel competent or decide much else.

He received a sophisticated building set and completed several models by following instructions. When asked to design something original, he became frustrated and put the pieces away, unsure how to begin without knowing the finished shape.

Remote school left him with plenty of space and few nearby peers. He watched cooking videos but rarely used the kitchen until his brother challenged him to make a complete breakfast without asking adults for each next step.

He began baking biscuits on Sundays and liked repeating a familiar recipe. A teacher encouraged him to document variations; Wyatt resisted at first, then became interested when a slightly different method actually changed the texture.

A family trip included a crowded city market that made him both uncomfortable and curious. He later asked to join a school service outing and enjoyed sorting supplies, while realizing he had never before followed a bus timetable.

He now bakes, plays casual online games, and helps with routine supply sorting several times a semester. College is assumed at home, but he cannot yet name what he wants from it besides friendships and a chance to become less dependent on familiar arrangements.

avoids: Open-ended tasks without an entry point
ambitions: Expects to pursue further education
Imagines a comfortable home but wants to learn how to run its ordinary routines himself.

biography.selfDescription: I know a lot of things are available to me, but available isn't the same as familiar. I'd like to get better at trying something before I decide that feeling awkward means I don't like it.
openQuestions: Would a less familiar environment broaden choices or initially reinforce avoidance?
Does repetition appeal independently of having a clear recipe?

biography.name: Lucía Benítez

background.family: Lives with parents and three siblings on a small leased farm; adults divide work and protect children’s study hours.
background.finances: Income from produce sales and a parent’s part-time clinic job covers basics but changes with weather and demand.
background.geography: Near Uvalde, Texas, with monthly trips to San Antonio for extended-family visits and events.
background.cultureLanguages: Mexican immigrant parents; Spanish and English are used throughout daily life, with relatives holding several different educational histories.
background.school: Homeschooled through an accredited distance program, with a local co-op for labs and group projects.
background.accessOpportunities: Has outdoor practical experience, borrowed instruments, and reliable but limited rural internet; wider opportunities require substantial travel.

timeline.story: Lucía helped sort tomatoes by color while inventing names for the misshapen ones. She liked talking with customers at a farm stand but also hid under the table to draw when conversations went on too long.

She learned to read in both household languages and enjoyed comparing how relatives told the same joke. A neighbor introduced her to a battered accordion, and she liked discovering tunes by testing buttons rather than reading notation.

A co-op experiment about soil drainage connected familiar field observations to a more formal question. Lucía enjoyed comparing jars but grew impatient with a classmate who recorded slowly, then realized that the slower notes were easier to understand later.

During remote community gatherings she recorded songs for relatives and learned to trim the beginning and end of clips. Farm routines continued, giving structure to days when screen lessons seemed detached from weather and seasons outside.

She tried a city music workshop during a family visit and found ensemble timing difficult. Instead of quitting, she asked the instructor for a recording to practice with at home and returned more prepared the following month.

A produce-order mix-up led her to help redesign the farm’s pickup sheet with clearer names and quantities. She liked the improvement but did not want every skill she learned to become another permanent family business duty.

Lucía studies chemistry through the co-op, practices borrowed accordion, and helps at selected market shifts. Texas colleges and technical programs are possibilities she can name, though she wants more firsthand experience before deciding whether to stay near land, music, both, or neither.

ambitions: Wants firsthand postsecondary exploration
Imagines a home with music and outdoor access, while remaining unsure how rural it should be.

biography.selfDescription: I like knowing what the weather changed, and I also like making a sound that has nothing to do with the farm. I want to learn more before deciding which parts of home I want to carry into my own daily life.
openQuestions: Would she enjoy formal scientific work away from familiar land?
How much group music can she sustain with travel constraints?

biography.name: Amara Chen

background.family: Lives with her two mothers and an older cousin attending community college; family conversation includes teasing and deliberate turn-taking.
background.finances: Comfortable income with reliable health coverage and enough savings for modest travel.
background.geography: Houston, Texas, near a light rail route.
background.cultureLanguages: Chinese American and white family connections; English and some Mandarin, with American Sign Language learned after her hearing difference was identified.
background.school: Public magnet school; bilateral hearing loss is accommodated with hearing technology, captioning, preferential seating, and written instructions.
background.accessOpportunities: Houston City College, museums, accessible theater events, and university outreach are nearby; she checks captioning before registering.

timeline.story: Amara liked dramatic puppet voices and lining up blocks by weight rather than color. Family members noticed she missed speech from another room, leading to hearing assessments and support that became an ordinary part of home routines.

She learned sign alongside spoken language and enjoyed making up visual jokes with a cousin. Her first school play went well because movements and lines were rehearsed, although she missed backstage directions in the noisy hallway.

An accessible museum workshop introduced simple circuits. She preferred taking turns testing components to a free-for-all building table. At home she dismantled a broken fan with permission and carefully labeled pieces she could not identify.

A teacher encouraged her to present a science demonstration. She practiced where to stand so she could see questions. Classmates' interest felt good, but she disliked becoming the default speaker about all hearing differences.

She joined a community theater group and helped design visual rehearsal cues. A ceramics session interested her less than expected because she disliked wet clay on her wrists, despite loving finished pottery.

Amara ran lighting for a short production and learned to ask for written changes before rehearsals. She also took a city gardening course, enjoying soil work with gloves and keeping meticulous germination notes.

She is preparing a public demonstration with captions and visual explanations while tending container vegetables. She feels confident onstage but is still learning to interrupt politely when access arrangements fail, especially with adults who insist they are speaking loudly enough.

motivations: Finding out why a setup works
ambitions: Build a reliable portable demonstration
Grow enough herbs to share
She imagines an adult home near accessible public places, with time to garden and share performances with friends.
struggles: Pressure to represent a whole community
practicalConstraints: Needs reliable captions and visual communication
Some events require advance accommodation requests

biography.selfDescription: I like an audience when we can all follow what is happening. I do not always want to explain my hearing, but I am good at explaining a circuit or why a scene needs different light.
openQuestions: How will she evaluate access in unfamiliar training settings?
Which part of demonstrations matters most: design, explanation, or performance?

biography.name: Isaac Han

background.family: Lives with his parents and a younger sister; family education decisions are discussed openly and revisited each year.
background.finances: Comfortable income from engineering and a small appliance-repair business, with some seasonal variation.
background.geography: Outside Waco, Texas.
background.cultureLanguages: Korean American family using English and Korean; he reads Korean more slowly than he speaks it.
background.school: Structured home education through a live online program, with fixed assignments, exams, and a weekly in-person cooperative.
background.accessOpportunities: McLennan Community College events, library classes, and regional campus visits are reachable; many daily peers are online rather than nearby.

timeline.story: Isaac liked pretending to run a restaurant and asking adults for detailed orders. He enjoyed making signs but would abandon a toy building project if nobody wanted to use the finished structure.

His family chose home education after finding a schedule that worked around both parents' jobs. He liked the predictable mornings and cooperative afternoons, especially cooking activities where everyone's contribution could be tasted.

He learned embroidery from an older neighbor and became patient with tiny stitches. His parents offered robotics materials, assuming he might enjoy them, but he preferred making fabric covers and instruction cards for the kit.

An online class gave him fixed deadlines and classmates in other states. He enjoyed discussing novels but struggled when jokes in the chat moved faster than he could follow. The in-person cooperative remained an important weekly anchor.

He helped run a cooperative snack table and liked remembering regular customers' preferences. A biology dissection interested him intellectually but felt unpleasant to handle. He wanted to learn the material through diagrams afterward rather than avoid it entirely.

Isaac began making embroidered patches for friends and underestimated how long paid requests would take. He refunded two orders and reduced the number he accepted. He also joined an improvised theater workshop, enjoying quick character choices despite initial reluctance.

He now balances scheduled coursework, a few patch commissions, and theater games. He is curious about a college classroom, partly for new people rather than a particular subject. His family supports exploration beyond the technical interests outsiders expect them to share.

avoids: Handling dissection specimens when alternatives are available
ambitions: Try an in-person college enrichment class
He imagines living among people who drop by for food and conversation, while keeping a quiet corner for detailed work

biography.selfDescription: People ask about engineering because of my parents, but I would rather show them something I stitched. I like a clear school schedule and a very unpredictable theater game.
openQuestions: How would he experience a large daily classroom?
Would craft commissions remain enjoyable at a larger volume?

biography.name: Jonas Loke

background.family: Lives with his parents and two sisters; an aunt and cousins in Beaumont host occasional visits and maintain frequent video calls.
background.finances: Modest stable income from a small delivery business and school cafeteria work.
background.geography: A small town outside Salem, Oregon.
background.cultureLanguages: Marshallese American family using Marshallese and English; household members differ in how much community activity they want each week.
background.school: Public high school with agricultural science, choir, and a regional vocational partnership.
background.accessOpportunities: Local community college events are easiest; Lamar-area public programs during Texas family visits are plausible, with nonresident costs and distance unresolved.

timeline.story: Jonas liked helping load empty boxes into the family van and asking which house came next. At home he planted seeds from fruit and was surprised that most did not sprout.
A school garden gave him a more reliable way to grow things. He enjoyed measuring leaves and disliked the competitive classroom chart that treated the tallest plant as the best.

He joined a children's choir and discovered he liked singing with others more than speaking alone. A cousin taught him simple video editing, but he preferred recording plant growth to making fast entertaining clips.

Jonas helped his parents plan a delivery route and enjoyed the practical geography. Customers' small talk felt awkward until he learned a few opening questions. He also began making tiny paper sculptures while listening to music.

A vocational workshop introduced welding, which relatives expected him to enjoy. He liked the precision but not the heat and protective clothing. He chose a horticulture elective afterward, without deciding whether that meant anything about future study.

He visited cousins in Beaumont and toured a community garden and public campus event. Humid-weather plants fascinated him. Back home he helped younger students compare growing conditions and learned to stop correcting every imperfect measurement immediately.

Jonas sings in choir, works in the school greenhouse, and occasionally rides delivery routes with a parent. He is considering a longer Texas visit but does not know whether the appeal is family, unfamiliar plants, or the idea of a different landscape.

avoids: Treating growth as a simple competition
motivations: Understanding why living things respond differently
Maintaining family connections without copying every family interest
ambitions: Compare the same plant in two climates
He imagines an adult home with room to grow plants and sing with other people, though he is unsure how far from family to live
struggles: Quiet participation can hide how much he knows

biography.selfDescription: I do not mind repeating an observation if something living keeps changing. I like a group sound better than a solo, but I still want people to notice my part.
openQuestions: Would he enjoy horticultural work when it includes routine commercial demands?
What would a longer stay away reveal about his preferred distance from family?

biography.name: Colton Reed

background.family: Lives with his father and grandmother; his mother lives elsewhere and calls irregularly.
background.finances: Basic expenses are usually covered, but unexpected repairs consume savings. He has a small amount from weekend chores.
background.geography: Outside a small town near Childress in the Texas Panhandle.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking extended family with strong local ties and frequent teasing that he does not always enjoy.
background.school: Small public high school; several activities share one afternoon bus.
background.accessOpportunities: Neither parent attended college. His grandmother keeps school paperwork organized. Colton has ADHD and describes losing track of materials even for activities he wants to do.

timeline.story: Colton wanted to carry a flashlight during every evening walk with his grandmother, even before dark. He collected smooth stones and abandoned them in coat pockets. At home he enjoyed cooking scrambled eggs with help but refused to taste the tomatoes his father kept offering him.

He and a friend swapped trading cards at recess, arguing about bent corners and whether a shiny card was really rare. Colton sometimes accepted a trade too quickly and regretted it later. He also loved a classroom singing game despite insisting at home that singing was embarrassing.

His father brought home a box of secondhand sports equipment. Colton cleaned several items and compared them with pictures in store flyers. He was disappointed that a carefully scrubbed glove still smelled musty. He played baseball that spring, then became more interested in bicycling with two neighbors.

For a school project he compared the price and quantity of several packages of seeds. He liked noticing that the largest package was not always cheapest per packet. The presentation arrived a day late because he left it on the kitchen table, a problem his good calculations did not solve.

He tried selling a few cleaned secondhand game accessories to people his family knew. One item did not work consistently, and refunding the buyer used most of what he had earned. He disliked admitting the mistake and avoided another sale for months, while continuing to browse listings for fun.

Colton compared three offers for supplies used at a school booth, including delivery costs that a friend initially ignored. He also underestimated how many boxes they could carry. His ADHD was already known at school; a checklist helped with some handoffs, but he still forgot it when rushing.

He is experimenting with occasional resale of used board games, checking missing pieces at the kitchen table. He enjoys comparing what different sellers include and is less interested in photographing each box. A recent game has attracted no buyers. He alternates between lowering its price and deciding he might keep it.

enjoys: Checking secondhand games for missing pieces
avoids: Admitting an item was a poor purchase
demonstratedSkills: Spotting differences in what sellers include
Testing used items before another person receives them
unfamiliarActivities: Keeping records for an entire year
Buying a large quantity of anything
Managing transactions with strangers at a distance
ambitions: Save for a dependable used vehicle
Try a larger town for a while
Have more control over his weekly schedule
struggles: Can conceal mistakes until asked directly
supports: A teacher who checks that he recorded instructions
practicalConstraints: Unfamiliarity with options after high school

biography.selfDescription: Comparing stuff is interesting. Posting it and waiting for answers is mostly annoying. People act like those are the same activity.
openQuestions: Will he keep wanting to do the less interesting parts?
How much financial uncertainty can he tolerate without withdrawing?

biography.name: Elena Vela

background.family: Lives with her father, grandmother, and younger brother; household responsibilities are negotiated day by day.
background.finances: Income fluctuates with available shifts and seasonal repairs. A replacement phone screen is a serious expense.
background.geography: Outside a small town in the Texas Panhandle, beyond the regular town bus route.
background.cultureLanguages: English at school, English and Spanish with her grandmother; understands more Spanish than she confidently speaks.
background.school: Small public school with one mathematics sequence per grade and no advanced mathematics option this year.
background.accessOpportunities: Uses borrowed library books and downloaded pages; home internet sometimes disappears for several days. No competition experience.

timeline.story: Elena arranged bottle caps along the kitchen grout and objected when her brother moved one. Her grandmother remembers a tidy child; Elena remembers wanting to know whether a row could have a middle without having an odd number. Neither account quite replaces the other.

During long drives into town, she invented counting rules for fence posts, sometimes counting only every third post and then restarting. She disliked being asked to demonstrate for visiting adults. At school she liked recess games but argued privately about rules that changed after someone lost.

A library book mentioned a number that could not be written as a fraction. She could follow some examples but not the explanation, and copied a paragraph onto feed-store receipt paper. The paper lived under her mattress until the ink faded; nobody assigned this investigation.

When the family connection stopped working, Elena made paper mazes with restrictions about crossing a line twice. Most failed, and she sometimes tore them up rather than explain the restriction. She also learned to cook eggs for her brother and resented losing uninterrupted afternoons.

She began experiencing persistent anxiety, including a racing heart before ordinary school presentations. A counselor met with her twice before moving away. Mathematics did not cause the anxiety or remove it; she still voluntarily spent evenings wondering which invented rules produced a pattern and which produced a mess.

Elena borrowed an old textbook and skipped between chapters without understanding their sequence. She made a table testing a claim about prime numbers, found an exception, and felt pleased enough to tell her father during dishes. She declined an online contest because connection problems and being timed both bothered her.

She now keeps a notebook labeled Questions Nobody Asked, containing unfinished arguments about infinity alongside grocery totals. Her teacher sometimes checks an argument but has little spare time. Elena wants more difficult material and also wants dependable money, without knowing how extended study could fit the household timetable.

enjoys: Inventing mathematical restrictions and looking for exceptions
Quiet card games with her grandmother
Walking the gravel road at dusk
avoids: Being described as a natural genius
Group chats that require immediate replies
activities: Does occasional paid fence painting with a neighbor
Downloads reading at the town library
demonstratedSkills: Finds counterexamples in her own tables
Explains the difference between a guess and an argument
Keeps younger brother on a workable evening routine
unfamiliarActivities: Sustained work in a large group
motivations: Understanding whether a statement must be true
Having choices without abandoning family obligations
ambitions: Work through a book she currently finds too difficult
Spend several uninterrupted days studying somewhere quiet

biography.selfDescription: “I like the part where an example breaks my rule. I do not like people watching me wait for an idea.”
openQuestions: Would she enjoy sustained formal instruction as much as private puzzles?
Which family responsibilities would remain hers if her schedule changed?
How would she respond to collaborative work without a timer?

biography.name: Marisol Peña

background.family: Lives with her parents, younger brother, and a cousin; neither parent attended college, and both ask practical questions about further education.
background.finances: Rent and routine bills are covered through combined wages, with little room for unpaid travel or expensive programs.
background.geography: Rio Grande Valley town near irrigated fields and growing retail strips.
background.cultureLanguages: Spanish at home and English at school; translates some ordinary written notices for relatives.
background.school: Public school with a busy biology teacher and limited laboratory supplies.
background.accessOpportunities: Public library, school reading access, backyard plants, and basic classroom experiments; no direct experience in care settings.

timeline.story: Marisol watched a scraped knee change color over several days and asked why the new surface looked different. She also pulled apart seed pods in the yard. Her mother remembers the mess more clearly than the questions, because Marisol often left the pieces on the kitchen table.

When bean plants grew at different speeds, she moved the slowest one closer to the window and forgot that she had changed its conditions. A teacher asked what else might explain the difference. Marisol began leaving little notes beside pots, though watering still happened whenever someone remembered.

She became curious about why breathing sped up after running, comparing her own recovery after different playground games. She did not make a formal record and sometimes confused effort with speed. An illustrated library book gave her new words and also made clear how many pieces she had missed.

Marisol read about digestion beyond the pages assigned in class and asked why explanations used both chemical and mechanical processes. Her teacher could answer part of the question. She copied unfamiliar words into a notebook, leaving blanks where the definitions assumed other knowledge she did not yet have.

A classroom experiment involving yeast caught her attention because a small change produced a visible difference. She repeated a rough version at home with uneven measuring spoons. She was more interested in what living systems were doing than in arranging a display, and admitted that her home comparison was unreliable.

She began borrowing books about regulation within bodies and reading beyond class even when the material was slow. Her parents worried about how long further study might take. Marisol said explicitly that many years of study would be acceptable if the subject kept opening up, although she could not explain the costs.

She now reads in short stretches between helping with dinner and a weekend paid shift packing produce. She wants deeper study of bodily and living systems and remains open to a lengthy education. She has never spent time in a care setting and cannot say whether those daily environments would suit her.

enjoys: Reading about feedback and regulation in living systems
Finding links between separate body processes
Growing plants with notes about changed conditions
avoids: Claiming her home experiments prove too much
Being rushed to name a final destination
Graphic videos shared mainly to shock people
activities: Packs produce during some weekend shifts
demonstratedSkills: Stays with difficult reading and marks missing prerequisites
Distinguishes a rough comparison from a controlled experiment
Explains linked processes using simple drawings
motivations: Understanding how living parts maintain a changing whole
Learning enough to replace memorized fragments with explanations
ambitions: Be the first in her immediate family to complete further education
Continue studying for many years if the questions remain compelling
Take a course with more substantial laboratory access
supports: Parents encourage education while asking about costs

biography.selfDescription: “A long time studying does not scare me as much as pretending I understand something because I remembered its name.”
openQuestions: How will interest change with more rigorous practical work?
Would she enjoy the routines and interpersonal demands of care settings?
What financial and family arrangements could support lengthy study?

biography.name: Tessa Walker

background.family: Stays with an aunt and two cousins while her mother moves between temporary arrangements; contact is frequent but plans change.
background.finances: Little spare money and no stable place to store possessions.
background.geography: Currently near Killeen, Texas, after several moves within the state.
background.cultureLanguages: English-speaking family; different households have different rules and traditions.
background.school: Third public school in two years, with incomplete activity records.
background.accessOpportunities: School-day opportunities and a phone with intermittent service; no dependable after-school ride or consistently available trusted adult.

timeline.story: Tessa remembers drawing on cereal boxes beside her mother and taking a long time to choose a cartoon. Family photographs suggest she enjoyed playground swings. She does not remember having one favorite activity and becomes uncomfortable when adults expect a clear story about what she has always loved.

She liked eating lunch beside the same two children and making up ridiculous names for their snacks. An after-school dance class was mentioned but never arranged. She sometimes borrowed her cousin’s crayons, although she was more interested in copying a funny face than filling every page.

A move interrupted friendships and changed the bus route. Tessa played simple phone games and watched her cousin braid hair, occasionally trying a braid herself. She declined a school performance because rehearsals required rides, but now cannot separate that practical problem from whether performing would have felt unpleasant.

Remote school was difficult when several people shared devices. She completed some work on paper and missed other lessons. Leisure mostly meant television, walks to a nearby shop, and sending voice messages. She liked choosing music for cleaning but had no equipment or opportunity to try making it.

Tessa helped younger cousins get snacks and sometimes invented a quiet guessing game. She liked them on some afternoons and wanted to be left alone on others. A teacher suggested a club without explaining its meetings. Tessa did not attend and remembers feeling too new to ask basic questions.

Housing changes meant packing possessions into bags twice in one year. She stopped keeping craft materials because carrying them became annoying. At one school she enjoyed a short cooking lesson; at another she avoided signing up because the return transport was unclear. Neither experience tells her much about a lasting preference.

Tessa currently watches comedy clips, walks with a cousin, and sometimes helps prepare rice and eggs. She would like an ordinary week with predictable space and transport. When asked about unfamiliar activities she often says she does not know, then worries that people interpret the answer as refusing to try.

enjoys: Walking to the corner shop with her cousin
avoids: Signing up when transport is uncertain
Keeping supplies she may have to move suddenly
activities: Helps with some meals and cousin supervision
Exchanges voice messages with an old friend
demonstratedSkills: Can prepare a few simple meals
Notices when younger cousins need a quieter activity
motivations: Would like chances to try things without a long commitment
ambitions: Finish this school year in one place
Have a small shelf that stays hers
struggles: Difficulty separating dislike from inaccessible circumstances
Reluctance to ask adults for help again
supports: A cousin who checks on schoolwork sometimes
An acquaintance who shares class notes

biography.selfDescription: I know what I do after school, but that is mostly what is there. I am tired of picking something on a form when I have never done it. Sometimes I do not want to do anything, and sometimes I would if getting there were simple.
openQuestions: Which activities would she choose with reliable access?
Which preferences persist when housing is settled?
What would a low-pressure first try look like?
